articles.body: NEW DELHI: BJP MP Sudhanshu Trivedi on Wednesday accused certain opposition forces of attempting to destabilise India under the guise of legitimate public demands, alleging that their ultimate objective was “regime change” through violence and conspiracy.Referring to the Prime Minister’s Vijayadashami address, Trivedi said certain forces were driven by three agendas: exploiting power for personal gain, creating divisions within society, and harbouring hatred towards Indian culture and religion.“These are the forces that seek to divide society, plunder state resources, and harbor animosity toward Indian culture and the Hindu faith. They organize conferences calling for the 'eradication of Sanatan Dharma,' spearhead global campaigns to 'dismantle Hindutva,' and propagate misleading narratives about India’s institutions. These are the very forces that do not wish to see India progress,” he said.Trivedi questioned the recurring demands and allegations concerning institutions such as LIC, HAL, SBI and SEBI, as well as vaccines, electronic voting machines (EVMs) and electoral rolls.Comparing the repeated demands to Ravana’s ten heads, he said, “In reality, much like Ravana, who possessed ten heads, if one head were severed, another would immediately emerge. Their demands are similar: satisfy one demand, and another will promptly take its place.”He argued that the common language used across various movements could help identify what he described as their underlying agenda. Drawing a parallel with Ravana disguising himself as an ascetic before abducting Sita, Trivedi alleged that certain forces were concealing their intentions behind seemingly legitimate demands.“In the Ramayana, when Ravana arrived to abduct Mata Sita, he did not appear in his true, demonic form, but rather disguised himself as an ascetic. Today, various forces are operating under such disguises, cloaked in deception. Their true objective is not the specific demands they present... their singular goal is 'regime change' through violent conflict and calculated conspiracy,” he said.Trivedi criticised those claiming the legacy of Shiv Sena founder Balasaheb Thackeray for allegedly aligning with forces that seek to undermine Indian religion and culture.“It is truly bizarre that those who claim to be the rightful heirs to the legacy of the highly revered Balasaheb Thackeray have now aligned themselves with the very forces that seek to destroy our religion and culture, and they state this with great conviction that 'Let him come from Vietnam, then 'regime change' will happen',” he said.Trivedi also questioned what Sanjay Raut knew about Rahul Gandhi that even Congress leaders were allegedly unaware of. “What is this 'lead,' this 'secret,' or this 'information' that Sanjay Raut possesses regarding Rahul Gandhi, something that even the Congress party's own leaders are unaware of? What kind of conspiratorial threads are these?” he asked.He further questioned the significance of references to developments following overseas visits, citing remarks about dropping a “hydrogen bomb”, predicting a “tsunami” and Raut’s comments. Trivedi alleged that such statements pointed to the involvement of unidentified and suspicious entities seeking to destabilise India.“Whether it is talk of dropping a 'hydrogen bomb' upon returning from abroad, or predicting a 'tsunami' after such a visit, and now these remarks by Sanjay Raut, all of this suggests that these actions are being orchestrated by unknown, suspicious entities, forces from across the border that seek to incite unrest within our nation,” he said.Expressing confidence in the government's position, Trivedi said the alleged attempt at “regime change” would fail under Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s leadership, backed by public trust and a commitment to the country.The remarks come amid a political row over calls for “regime change” by opposition leaders and student activists during ongoing protests in Delhi against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.Senior advocate Prashant Bhushan, All India Students Association (AISA) president Neha Bora and Congress spokesperson Pawan Khera have used or discussed the phrase at conferences and press briefings linked to the protests.Earlier, Shiv Sena (UBT) chief Uddhav Thackeray backed the calls, arguing that denying people the right to express their views through elections and protests would leave them with no option but to seek a change of government.BJP on Tuesday also intensified its attack on Lok Sabha Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi over his alleged visit to Vietnam amid opposition protests against the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. The US envoy arrived in Russia with fresh proposals aimed at bringing Moscow and Kyiv back to the negotiating table.The discussions covered several issues beyond Ukraine, including the release of an American prisoner, renewed US-Russia economic cooperation, Russian diesel exports and the possibility of a meeting between Putin and US President Donald Trump in China.Ukraine peace proposals and trilateral talksWitkoff presented documents outlining possible ways to settle the Ukraine conflict, according to Russian news agency Interfax. He also urged Putin to consider resuming trilateral talks involving Russia, Ukraine and the United States to address technical issues surrounding a potential peace agreement.A US official told CNN that Washington and Kyiv had made "meaningful progress" during Tuesday's discussions in Norway."Discussions covered key elements of a comprehensive peace framework, including long-term security guarantees for Ukraine, a post-war economic and prosperity plan, and a broader European security architecture designed to create lasting stability," the official said.Release of 74-year-old American prisonerRussia also released Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired American teacher from Michigan who had been imprisoned on charges of fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine.Hubbard was sentenced to nearly seven years in prison following a closed trial in 2024. Russian prosecutors alleged that he had signed a contract with the Ukrainian military after Moscow launched its invasion in February 2022 and fought alongside Ukrainian forces until his capture two months later.The Biden administration had designated Hubbard as wrongfully detained.Witkoff thanked Putin for his release, saying, "Because of you, he's going home to his family." Putin confirmed that Hubbard was at St Petersburg's Pulkovo airport following his release.Possible Putin-Trump meeting in ChinaPutin proposed meeting Trump in China, according to Russian state television, as quoted by Reuters. The Kremlin had previously raised the possibility of trilateral talks involving Putin, Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China next month. No agreement on a meeting was immediately announced.US-Russia economic cooperation and diesel exportsPutin also raised the possibility of restoring economic cooperation between Moscow and Washington. The discussions came as Russia prepared to dispatch its first diesel shipment to the United States on Thursday following an agreement with Trump.Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said the initial shipment would carry 40,000 metric tons of diesel, with further supplies expected."Additional shipments will follow, of course. There were agreements reached between the two leaders. We will meet the United States' needs, to the extent of our capabilities," Novak said, according to RIA.Witkoff also thanked Putin for lifting restrictions on Russian diesel exports, while Putin said diesel prices had declined following the agreement.Iran war and other discussionsThe two sides also discussed Russia's willingness to help resolve the war in Iran, according to footage of the meeting reported by CNN.Potential Russian fertiliser exports to the United States were among the other issues raised during the discussions, reflecting efforts to explore broader economic engagement alongside diplomatic negotiations.Why the meeting mattersThe meeting comes at a critical juncture in Washington's efforts to broker a settlement between Russia and Ukraine, with the two sides remaining deeply divided over territory and security guarantees.Ukraine has insisted that any peace agreement must include credible guarantees against future Russian aggression and cannot require Kyiv to surrender territory.Moscow, meanwhile, continues to demand control over the entire Donbas region, a reduction in Ukraine's military strength and assurances that Kyiv will never join NATO.The talks also come amid growing strains between Washington and Kyiv following Trump's decision to waive sanctions on Russia under legislation aimed at restricting Moscow's war financing, alongside the agreement to import Russian diesel.Ahead of the meeting, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov warned that Moscow would not make "political concessions" and said Russia did "not expect a miracle" from Witkoff's visit.You use AI every day. articles.title: Paramilitary hitman linked to British right-wing group Turning Point UK
articles.summary: Al Jazeera exposes UK far right’s links to criminal underworld.
articles.body:
A violent paramilitary linked to a proscribed terror group has close ties to a right-wing student group in the United Kingdom, an Al Jazeera investigation has revealed.

Allan Nesbitt, a convicted criminal who is a member of the Ulster Volunteer Force (UVF), is linked to Turning Point UK (TPUK).

Our investigation, Contract Killers and the Far Right, began in 2021, when an undercover reporter from Al Jazeera joined TPUK, an independent offshoot of the right-wing US activist group Turning Point USA. TPUK has close ties to several senior British Conservative Party members, as well as to leaders of Reform UK.

TPUK’s CEO Jack Ross stood as a Conservative Party candidate in 2023. Ross introduced Al Jazeera’s undercover reporter to Nesbitt, who is from Glasgow, Scotland.

Ross made clear that he and Nesbitt had a long history together. Ross was filmed by our undercover reporter agreeing to pay Nesbitt thousands of pounds to stage a fake political rally designed to show support for the lifting of UK sanctions against Zimbabwe.

Ross also told Al Jazeera’s undercover operative that for “a certain amount”, Nesbitt and his contacts could arrange physical attacks, saying they could “kick the f*** out of someone. They can start cutting people’s faces up. That’s another amount. They can stab someone,” Ross said. “They can shoot someone. They could kill someone.”

To test Ross’s claims about Nesbitt, Al Jazeera’s undercover operative devised a story about a business dispute with a fictional rival they wanted “dealt with”.

In a private meeting in a London hotel, Nesbitt told our reporters he could “arrange whatever you need done”, but “at a price”. This included killing the fictional person with the help of his UVF connections.

“He can have a bad accident,” Nesbitt said, confirming to Al Jazeera that the person would be “finished”.

“These c***s are terrorists. They’re f***ing trained killers,” Nesbitt added.

Nesbitt also claimed to have personally killed before.

“Things have happened in the past where it was too risky to do that [gestures firing a gun], and I’ve just pulled out a knife and stabbed the c*** to death,” he said.

In a later video call, Nesbitt showed off a shotgun, a pistol, and live ammunition to prove he had the means to follow through.

The money paid for the murder would be used to arm the UVF in Northern Ireland, Nesbitt said.

“All the money gets raised in Scotland and the things get bought in Scotland and we smuggle them into Ireland.”

According to Nesbitt, he has been involved in this weapons smuggling for many years.

“It’s us that smuggled the stuff into Ireland for them to fight the war in there,” he said, referring to The Troubles .

During that period, which began in the late 1960s, Catholic and Protestant groups in Northern Ireland fought over whether Protestant-majority Northern Ireland should remain part of the UK or join the Catholic-majority Republic of Ireland.

Those in favour of Northern Ireland remaining a part of the UK are widely known as unionists or loyalists. Those seeking to break from the UK usually identify themselves as republicans or Irish nationalists.

The UVF belonged to the Protestant loyalist side and was responsible for some of the most infamous killings and murders during The Troubles, according to Patricia Devlin, a journalist who has been investigating the group for years.

“Between 1966 and 1999, the UVF killed over 500 people,” she told Al Jazeera.

“They went on to commit atrocities such as the 1971 McGurk’s bar bomb massacre, which killed 15 people, and the 1974 Dublin and Monaghan bombings, which killed 33 people”, she added.

But after the 1998 Good Friday Agreement that at least officially ended the Troubles, the UVF, like many other groups, transformed into a more traditional criminal gang.

“The movement has turned into drug gangs, while still using the name of the UVF,” Devlin said.

To Roy McComb, former deputy director of the UK’s National Crime Agency, Nesbitt’s claims are no surprise.

“The history of loyalism between Northern Ireland [and] Scotland is a very strong and very longstanding one.

“Operationally, there’s certainly evidence previously of firearms being trafficked, of intelligence being shared, of activists being moved between the two countries [Scotland and Northern Ireland].

“Firearms … are simply tools that can be sold and that could be sold onto the far right.”

Besides links to the UVF, Al Jazeera’s investigation also shows links between Turning Point UK and other far-right agitators in the UK. These include groups that have been at the forefront of protests against migrants and LGBTQ+ rights.

“Turning Point UK are fanboys of these kinds of people. These people are obviously a lot more physically tough than Turning Point UK. Turning Point UK know that they put these little, no far right allowed at the bottom just to protect themselves,” Ciaran O’Connor, senior analyst at the Institute for Strategic Dialogue, told Al Jazeera.

“They use these events as wedge issues upon which to try and mobilise their support and try and attack the message or the meaning of the other side, and demonise the housing of asylum seekers in society,” he added.

A former member of the UVF told Al Jazeera that the “far right in the UK is a toothless tiger”, but links between the far right and groups like the UVF could change that.

“It changes whenever you make a connection to individuals who are behind a terrorist campaign for probably 40 years, and are still armed, and still have the ability to shoot and bomb,” the former UVF member said.

Al Jazeera notified Scottish police about Allan Nesbitt and his weapons in the interest of public safety.

Jack Ross denied our findings “completely”, telling us that everything he said to our undercover reporter was not meant seriously.

The other parties featured did not respond to our inquiries.

articles.title: WW1 to Houthis: British jets for Saudi Arabia build on long military bond
articles.summary: UK’s deployment of jets to defend Saudi Arabia is the latest chapter in a relationship older than the kingdom itself.
articles.body:
The United Kingdom has announced it will deploy Royal Air Force Typhoon fighter jets to help defend Saudi Arabia from missile and drone attacks by Yemen’s Houthis, the armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God).

The jets will play a “defensive role”, the British Ministry of Defence (MoD) said in a statement on Tuesday, adding that they will not carry out attacks against the Iranian-backed armed group.

The move comes amid heavy fighting between the Houthis and Yemen’s internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia.

In recent weeks, the Houthis have carried out missile and drone attacks against the kingdom, including oil facilities and Riyadh’s main airport , while the Saudi-led coalition supporting the Yemeni government has launched air attacks on Houthi positions.

The UK’s decision to send jets to assist Saudi Arabia marks just the latest chapter in a partnership that stretches back more than a century, to a treaty signed during the First World War, years before the Saudi kingdom was founded.

So what is the UK sending, and how did the two countries become so closely bound?

Fighter jets, an A400M transport aircraft and advisers.

The ministry said it was also extending air-to-air refuelling , which it previously agreed to provide for Saudi air operations, including those to degrade Houthi military targets in Yemen.

How far back does the UK-Saudi relationship go?

In December 1915, Sir Percy Cox, a senior British official in the Gulf, concluded the Treaty of Darin with King Abdulaziz Ibn Saud, then ruler of Nejd in central Arabia, according to India Office records held by the UK’s National Archives.

In return, he allied with Britain against the Ottoman Empire, and Britain backed him with cash and weapons.

In May 1927, Britain signed a new treaty with him at Jeddah, according to an India Office memorandum.

King Abdulaziz founded the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in 1932.

In May 1966, Saudi Arabia signed contracts to buy 40 Lightning fighter jets and 25 jet trainers from the British Aircraft Corporation, along with a radar system, according to a US Department of State memo from the time.

Even then, Yemen was part of the picture.

In 1962, the Mutawakkilite Kingdom of Yemen was overthrown in a military coup and the Yemen Arab Republic was established. Egypt sent troops to back the republican government, while Saudi Arabia and Jordan armed and funded royalist forces trying to restore the Imam. By 1966, the civil war had reached a stalemate.

Meanwhile, Britain was facing rebellion from Soviet- and Egypt-backed nationalist groups over its control of Aden and southern Yemen. Britain ultimately withdrew in 1967.

In 1966, Saudi Arabia’s defence minister, Prince Sultan, asked the UK to supply an RAF fighter squadron to fly under Saudi colours if fighting resumed in Yemen, according to declassified US State Department records.

Britain instead offered fighter jets flown by British pilots, and said it was ready to send an RAF squadron of Lightning interceptors for a short period if required.

In the end, Saudi Arabia accepted the jets and civilian pilots, and the RAF squadron was not needed, the records show.

BAE Systems, then the British Aircraft Corporation, says its ties with Saudi Arabia date back to 1966, and in 1973, the two governments signed a memorandum of understanding naming the company as prime contractor.

In 1985, the two governments signed an oil-for-arms agreement, known as Al-Yamamah, for Tornado and Hawk jets.

The Reuters news agency has described the Al-Yamamah deals as the largest export contracts in British history.

Saudi Arabia set aside up to 600,000 barrels of oil a day to pay for Tornado jets and other equipment.

The UK’s Serious Fraud Office investigated corruption allegations linked to the deal from 2004, but dropped the inquiry in December 2006, according to a House of Lords judgement.

The attorney general, Lord Goldsmith, cited the need to safeguard national security.

Has Britain fought from Saudi soil before?

When Iraq invaded Kuwait in August 1990, King Fahd of Saudi Arabia asked friendly governments for help.

On August 11, 12 RAF Tornado fighters flew from Akrotiri in Cyprus to Dhahran in Saudi Arabia, according to the RAF Museum.

Further RAF Tornado detachments were set up at Tabuk in Saudi Arabia in October 1990, and at Dhahran in January 1991, the museum’s records show.

During the war, then-Defence Secretary Tom King told Parliament that Saudi Arabia had provided the UK with host-nation support.

He also reported that a Tornado based in the kingdom had gone missing, the fourth lost in enemy action.

British aircraft then patrolled a no-fly zone over southern Iraq, alongside United States and French jets, flying from Saudi bases until 2003, according to the US Air Force.

In September 2007, Saudi Arabia agreed to buy 72 Typhoons from Britain, the UK MoD said at the time. The jets were to replace Tornadoes and other aircraft in the Saudi air force.

The deal was worth 4.43 billion pounds (then about $8.9bn).

BAE Systems, which builds the jets, called it the Salam Project.

Further RAF Tornado detachments were set up at Tabuk in Saudi Arabia in October 1990 and at Dhahran in January 1991.

In March 2018, during Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s visit to London, the UK signed a memorandum of intent with Saudi Arabia to finalise the purchase of 48 more Typhoons, BAE Systems said in a statement to the London Stock Exchange.

Germany, which helps build the Typhoon and has a veto over its exports, halted arms sales to Saudi Arabia after the killing of Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi , a columnist for The Washington Post who wrote critically of the crown prince and his policies, in 2018.

Berlin dropped its objection in January 2024, with then-Foreign Minister Annalena Baerbock saying the Middle East had become a completely different place since October 7, 2023, when southern Israel was attacked by Hamas and Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza .

BAE said that year it was supporting the UK government in discussions with Saudi Arabia.

In June 2019, five years after the Houthis seized Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, triggering a brutal civil war, the UK’s Court of Appeal ruled that the government had acted unlawfully by licensing arms sales to Saudi Arabia for possible use in Yemen without assessing whether past incidents had breached international humanitarian law.

New licences were halted. In July 2020, then-Trade Secretary Liz Truss told Parliament they would resume, saying there was not a clear risk the arms would be used in a serious violation of the law.

The UK has also struck the Houthis directly. RAF Typhoons joined US attacks on Yemen in 2024 following Houthi attacks on Israel-linked Red Sea shipping in response to the bombardment of Gaza, according to the MoD.

Then, in September this year, Britain sent a Voyager tanker to assist Saudi Arabia with air-to-air refuelling of fighter jets. The planes it refuels are British-built Typhoons flown by the Saudi air force.

articles.title: Why are French protesters chanting ‘Bismillah, c’est les ténèbres’?
articles.summary: The slogan has come to represent a whole array of grievances that lie at the heart of the protest movement.
articles.body:
As violent protests roil France, bringing together students demanding better educational conditions and groups rejecting the high cost of living, one chant has become an improbable rallying cry: “Bismillah, c’est les ténèbres”.

The unofficial slogan does not mean much taken literally, but students have channelled a whole array of grievances that lie at the heart of the protest movement into this nonsensical expression. It is meant to mock racial stereotyping by the police.

Hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets nationwide over the weekend, in the largest mobilisation since protests over education reforms and rising prices began last month. The protest movement has been triggered by grievances ranging from overcrowded classrooms and teacher shortages to systemic inequality and lack of opportunity.

Police conduct has also come under scrutiny. France’s police inspectorate, the IGPN, has opened dozens of investigations into alleged police violence since protests began.

“Bismillah” is Arabic for “in the name of God”, an expression used by Muslims before beginning an activity. In French slang, it has lost some of its original meaning, becoming more akin to “let’s do it”.

“C’est les ténèbres” literally translates as “it’s the darkness”, which alludes to a situation that is bleak and hopeless.

The slogan therefore translates as “In the name of God, it’s the darkness”, which does not convey a clear message in and of itself.

Students say the phrase is a mockery of the police force, which tried to infiltrate social media chats used by protesters to coordinate.

The screenshot of a Snapchat conversation featuring the expression began circulating in early October. In it, a user named Mamadou requests to be added to a group, saying: “Hi, in the name of God, it’s the darkness. When’s the blockade, wallah, bro?”

The message also featured emojis with Algerian flags.

Students say the message was sent by undercover police officers attempting to infiltrate their chats by using an unconvincing mix of Arabic and slang. The claim has not been verified and French authorities have not issued any statement.

Youssef El Chazli, associate professor in Arab and Mediterranean sociology at Paris 8 University Vincennes – Saint-Denis, said the phrase “reinforces an image of out-of-touch policemen filled with stereotypes”.

“Such stereotypes appear to disproportionately aim at youths from Arab and African descent,” El Chazli told Al Jazeera. “This appears as one more example of how out-of-touch state agencies seem to be with the current movement.”

What does the slogan tell us about the protest movement?

The slogan has appeared on cardboard placards as a mockery of racial stereotypes and as a symbol of how authorities are out of touch with the realities of young people.

The slogan has spread as far as Italy and Belgium, where similar protests over the high cost of living and poor education also took place over the weekend.

El Chazli said satirical memes and internet trends have become tools to express political grievances during protests, which have traditionally been “inventive and creative”. “With youth mobilisations, protest creativity will draw heavily on youths’ subcultures,” he said.

Discussions around Islamophobia have also taken a front seat in public debate. French authorities have been reluctant to comment publicly on a significant spike in Islamophobic acts in France. One report cited by the Reuters news agency last year showed a 72 percent increase in such incidents during the January-March quarter of 2025 compared with the same period in 2024.

The French far right quickly resorted to racist language to blame Muslim youths for the violence, while United States President Donald Trump also chimed in, claiming that this is about “Islam wanting to take over”.

“What used to be a nonsubject 20 years ago is now a debated point,” El Chazli said. “For younger generations, Arab and African influences have been steadily mainstreaming in youth subcultures, owing to sports and arts figures, as well as new radio shows or social media content.”

articles.title: DAN HOFFMAN: Grief can break your heart. Here's how to keep it from breaking your life
articles.summary: Marcus Aurelius' Stoic wisdom frames a CIA veteran's journey through grief after losing his wife Kim to cancer and raising their sons alone.
articles.body: Roman emperor and Stoic philosopher Marcus Aurelius once said, "If thou art pained by any external thing, it is not this thing that disturbs thee, but thy own judgment about it." If there is one thing my sons and I learned from my late wife Kim's fight against cancer, it was how to distinguish between traumatic life events over which we have no control and the power we have to respond to them as we choose. A few weeks ago, my sons and I watched "White Room," a short introspective film directed by JT Rees. The film tells the story of 24-year-old Reese, who has tried for years to avoid dealing with his feelings over his older sister Joy's death. But grief has a way of lingering in our hearts while gnawing away at our inner peace. The movie is about sibling love and coming to terms with the loss of Reese’s older sister. 'DEADPOOL' STAR ROB DELANEY REVEALS HOW LOSING 2-YEAR-OLD SON CHANGED HIS APPROACH TO FAME "White Room" is based on JT's own life experience. When he was 9 years old, he lost his 12-year-old sister Jessie to brain cancer. My sons and I never met Jessie Rees, but we have bonded deeply with her family over shared grief from losing loved ones to cancer. And for years, we've been soothing our broken hearts by partnering with the Jessie Rees Foundation to support kids in the fight for their lives against pediatric cancer. CANCER TREATMENT DELAYS SURGE ACROSS US AS DOCTOR WARNS SYSTEM ‘NEEDS FIXING IMMEDIATELY’ We were always a close-knit family, but now it was the three of us, whom my late wife Kim lovingly called "my boys," facing the post-traumatic stress Kim's fight against cancer had left in its wake. That's why we identified so profoundly with JT's alter ego and protagonist Reese when Joy showed him how to process his sorrow by understanding it was not his fault. Grief can paralyze us. But even if we have no control over the disease that took our loved one's life, we absolutely can make our own decisions about what to do about it. "I had cancer!" Joy screams. She comforts Reese and exhorts him never to give up. "It's OK to cry," Joy says. "I'll always be right here watching you. You know where to find me." AMANDA KLOOTS CONFRONTS BIGGEST MISCONCEPTION ABOUT DATING AFTER LOSING A SPOUSE Joy encourages Reese to "Live your life. Promise me you'll try." Grief can paralyze us. But even if we have no control over the disease that took our loved one's life, we absolutely can make our own decisions about what to do about it. I honor Kim's memory by fulfilling the promise I made to her on her deathbed to do my best to ensure our sons live their lives to the fullest while carrying with them the grief of losing their mom to cancer when they were only 8 and 11 years old. SON WHO LOST FATHER IN 9/11 ATTACKS SHARES POWERFUL LESSONS 25 YEARS LATER: ‘I’M STILL HERE’ And so, on the day after their mom passed away, my sons went to school just as they had throughout Kim's fight against cancer, including her last few months in hospice. They expressed their sorrow with the help of a service dog and art therapy. They went to swim practice and played outside with their friends. They've never stopped doing the things that make kids' lives fun and meaningful. Long before my wife was stricken with cancer, I learned that lesson about resilience while serving overseas with the CIA in a Middle East war zone. Upon returning late one night to our overseas field station from leave, I was informed at the airport that one of the CIA's most decorated, courageous and brilliant paramilitary officers had been killed in action. We held a memorial service and never stopped carrying in our hearts the grief over our loss. But we also got right back to our counterterrorism mission and honored our fallen colleague's memory by relentlessly taking the fight to the enemy as he would have wanted. MIKE SARRAILLE: EXTORTION 17'S HEROES DIED ONCE. AMERICA MUST NEVER LET THEM DIE TWICE And therein lies the meaning of the CIA's Memorial Wall in the lobby of the Original Headquarters Building. Every time I walked into CIA Headquarters, I would look up at the stars on the wall commemorating our fallen heroes and repeat the same ritual when I departed at the end of the day, always deep in thought about honoring the legacy of those we lost. "White Room" is a must-see film, especially for anyone who has experienced loss over which they never had any control and suffered all the collateral damage. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION My sons and I miss our Kim every day. But together we have learned how to discover and build resilience in our broken hearts. Do the work. Stay engaged. Don't run from your sadness. But let your grief shape how you honor the memory of the one you lost. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP And remember you're not alone. Your loved one is with you, an angel on your shoulders. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM DANIEL HOFFMAN

articles.title: ‘I'm not a travel agent’: Shashi Tharoor when asked about Rahul Gandhi's foreign trip
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Congress MP Shashi Tharoor on Wednesday declined to comment on Lok Sabha Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi’s overseas visit amid protests in
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress MP Shashi Tharoor on Wednesday declined to comment on Lok Sabha Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi’s overseas visit amid protests in New Delhi against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, saying, “I am not a travel agent.”“I am not a travel agent. There is no point in asking me that question. Why did I leave Delhi and come here now? Every person has certain responsibilities. So, I cannot comment on that,” Tharoor said when asked about Rahul’s travel plans.Tharoor’s remarks came after the BJP stepped up its criticism of Rahul Gandhi over his alleged foreign trip amid opposition protests in Delhi against the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. The BJP shared a video on X purportedly showing the Lok Sabha Leader of Opposition aboard a flight to Vietnam, saying, “Too tired of spreading lies. Let me tour Vietnam for a while, who would get to know.”BJP leader Shahnawaz Hussain also took a swipe at Gandhi, suggesting he needed a break after his activities during the protests.“Rahul ji was very tired. He worked very hard. Sometimes he went to a police station, sometimes he sat inside All India Radio, sometimes he lay down on the road to get his pictures clicked, sometimes he pushed and shoved police personnel, and sometimes he knocked a journalist to the ground. He works so hard that he gets exhausted,” Hussain said.Congress leader Sandeep Dikshit, however, defended Rahul’s right to travel abroad, questioning the BJP’s criticism.“Who travels where and when... what is the issue? Do others not travel abroad? Rahul Gandhi is an individual and the leader of the opposition. He has his duties. He interacts with students at Yale University, meets students in London and engages with intellectuals there. He even gives press interviews, something the Prime Minister does not do,” Dikshit said.He also cited Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s foreign visits during Parliament sessions, questioning why they had not drawn similar criticism.“We also have a tradition that the Prime Minister does not travel abroad when the Lok Sabha is in session. But our PM broke that tradition. Why does no question arise at that time?” he asked.Rahul has been leading the opposition’s campaign against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over the SIR exercise, demanding his resignation. The Election Commission and the BJP have rejected allegations of irregularities in the revision process, accusing Rahul of “spreading lies”.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: After her son died at 23 in 2016, Elaine Roberts and son-in-law Luke Ambler started a men's support group with nine attendees; today it helps 7,000 men a week and has earned a national award
articles.summary: In a world where men are often expected to keep their struggles to themselves, nine people gathered in Halifax in 2016 around an idea that was as ordinary
articles.body: In a world where men are often expected to keep their struggles to themselves, nine people gathered in Halifax in 2016 around an idea that was as ordinary as it was important. A decade later, that small meeting has grown into a nationwide support network reaching thousands of men every week, carrying forward the memory of a young man whose death changed his family forever. Scroll down to read the details of the unique concept.A personal loss becomes a missionAccording to the BBC report, Andrew Roberts was just 23 when he died by suicide on April 5, 2016. His death came as a devastating shock to his family, including his mother, Elaine Roberts, and his brother-in-law, former professional rugby league player Luke Ambler. In the months that followed, the two began to consider how other families might be spared a similar experience.Their response was Andy’s Man Club, a peer-support charity named in Andrew’s memory. The idea was to create an informal, welcoming space where men could discuss their problems without fear of judgement, formal referrals or the pressure of finding the right words. The emphasis was on conversation, connection and the reassurance that nobody had to face difficult moments alone.According to the BBC, the first meeting was held in Halifax in 2016, with nine men attending. What began as a small community initiative has since developed into a nationwide movement.From nine men to thousandsAndy’s Man Club now operates more than 350 community groups across England, Scotland and Wales, alongside online sessions. Its weekly meetings collectively support around 7,000 men, offering free, confidential, walk-in sessions without registration or a referral.The model relies on volunteers, many of whom first came to the club seeking support themselves. Having experienced the value of being heard, they return to help others navigate similar challenges. This cycle of mutual support makes those who needed help now part of the network that helps.One of the early attendees was Oliver Vikse, who had experienced homelessness, the breakdown of his family unit and the loss of three friends to suicide. Finding a place where he could speak openly and be listened to became an important turning point, demonstrating the need for spaces that make emotional honesty easier.Challenging the silence around men’s mental healthAmbler has also helped take the charity’s message beyond its weekly meetings through the #ItsOkayToTalk campaign. The initiative reached more than 100 million people worldwide, encouraging men to speak about their experiences and challenging the stigma associated with seeking support, adds BBC report.The need remains significant. Office for National Statistics data for 2024 showed that suicide in England and Wales was around three times more common among men than women. For Andy’s Man Club, addressing that imbalance means making support accessible, familiar and free from the barriers that can prevent people from reaching out.Elaine has also highlighted the importance of face-to-face contact at a time when everyday social interactions are increasingly shaped by digital communication. The club offers men an opportunity to meet others, build friendships and discover that struggles they may have considered deeply personal are not theirs alone.A decade of making a differenceThe charity’s growth has been recognised through a national award, reflecting the impact of a project built around one family’s determination to turn grief into action. The Pride of Britain website has highlighted the story of Elaine and Ambler, whose work has helped create a lasting legacy in Andrew’s name.As Andy’s Man Club marks its tenth anniversary, a commemorative mural is also being unveiled at Leeds Trinity Shopping Centre, inviting members of the public to contribute to the artwork. The installation celebrates the people who have shaped the charity over the past decade.From nine attendees in Halifax to thousands of men gathering every Monday, the organisation’s expansion illustrates how a simple conversation can become the foundation of something much larger. Its mission remains rooted in the same principle that inspired its creation: making it easier for men to talk, find support and feel connected before a difficult moment becomes a crisis.Image Courtesy: Pride of BritainYou use AI every day. articles.title: North Korea tells border troops to take ‘resolute action’ if South threatens their safety
articles.summary: North Korea has told its border troops to take “prompt ​and resolute action” if South Korean forces threaten their safety, state media ​said on Wednesday, raising the risk of a clash along the ⁠heavily armed frontier.
articles.body: North Korea has told its border troops to take “prompt ​and resolute action” if South Korean forces threaten their safety, state media ​said on Wednesday, raising the risk of a clash along the ⁠heavily armed frontier. The report came a day after Seoul pledged to punish “resolutely” any ​further provocation by Pyongyang if North Korea acted on threats to strengthen its military ​posture along the border. North Korean Army Marshal Pak Jong Chon inspected fortifications on the border with South Korea on Tuesday, accompanied by Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of leader Kim Jong ​Un, KCNA reported. Kim Yo Jong said new firepower units had “taken their firing positions” at ​the border, KCNA reported. Tensions between North and South Korea have risen since Pyongyang began fortifying its ‌border ⁠in April 2024. The two countries are separated by the Demilitarized Zone that was established when the Korean War ended in an armistice in 1953. Seoul says Pyongyang has sent up to 7,000 workers to the border this year, with about 50 ​crossings of the ​Military Demarcation Line, ⁠which bisects the DMZ, to South Korea’s side of the border. On Wednesday, North Korea rejected Seoul’s allegations, with Pak dismissing ​the claim as an “absurd assertion” designed to shift blame, KCNA reported. The ​North Korean ⁠army knew where the border lay “better than any others” and was only doing what it should within its own territory, Pak said, urging soldiers to turn the border ⁠into an “impregnable ​fortress.” South Korea said North Korean mines caused ​a border blast last month that seriously wounded two of its soldiers, and called on Pyongyang to suspend the ​fortification work.

articles.title: Weather: Irish weather warning ahead of Storm Austen
articles.summary: The Republic of Ireland's weather service warns of potential of flooding and travel disruption.
articles.body:
Weather warnings have been issued across the Republic of Ireland ahead of the arrival of Storm Austen from the Atlantic on Thursday.

The storm is forecast to track to the south coast on Thursday evening into Friday morning bringing the risk of flooding, travel disruption, and potentially dangerous conditions.

While no warnings have been issued for Northern Ireland, Storm Austen is expected to bring widespread rain on Thursday night, clearing east on Friday morning.

An orange warning – the second highest level – for rain has been issued for six counties, including Cork, Dublin, Kerry, Waterford, Wexford, and Wicklow.

Irish weather service Met Éireann has warned of the potential of flooding, public transport disruption, and very difficult driving conditions.

A nationwide yellow warning for rain and wind has also been issued from 19:00 local time on Thursday to 10:00 on Friday.

The arrival of Storm Austen is unlikely to mark the end of the unsettled weather.

Another area of low pressure is forecast to track to the north of Ireland over the coming weekend, bringing the potential for a further spell of wet and very windy weather right across the island.

While the exact impacts of this second weather system remain uncertain, its arrival means a possibility of several days of changeable and potentially disruptive conditions.

The UK's Met Office, Ireland's Met Éireann, and the Royal Netherlands Meteorological Institute (KNMI) jointly prepare an alphabetic list , including public suggestions.

A storm is named when medium or high impacts are expected in one of those countries, helping people recognise and respond to warnings.

The storm season runs from 1 September to 31 August, but the main period of storm activity is October to March.

Storms, however, can still occur outside these peak months.

Is climate change making storms stronger or more frequent?

Most projections suggest UK winter windstorms could become slightly more frequent and intense, although uncertainty remains.

Rising sea levels are also expected to worsen coastal flooding from storms.

articles.title: Astronaut Tim Peake's video leaves Plymouth pupils starstruck
articles.summary: The surprise came after a teacher's father met Peake while working on a cruise ship.
articles.body:
Primary school children have been left amazed after receiving a personal video message from British astronaut Tim Peake.

Pupils at Thornbury Primary School in Plymouth, Devon, were sent the message after teacher Emily Trevarthen's father met Peake while working on a cruise ship over the summer.

Trevarthen explained that her father and the astronaut got chatting and her father mentioned she was a teacher. "We didn't expect to get what we got really," she said.

Peake told pupils : "I hear you've been studying all about space, a subject very close to my heart, something I love, so I'm very pleased that you enjoy it too. Stay curious. Keep looking up at the stars."

Trevarthen said that some children had previously assumed all astronauts were American, but learning about a British astronaut had helped them see that such ambitions were possible.

The video was kept secret until World Space Week , when staff revealed it during a celebration assembly.

Trevarthen said the children were "so excited" when they saw the video, with some initially wondered whether the message had been created using artificial intelligence before realising it was genuine.

She said: "The children absolutely loved it. The standout moment was learning that Tim Peake had run a marathon on the International Space Station. They couldn't believe it."

Teacher Joanna Stelmaszczyk said there was "so much excitement" when the video was shown and recalled similar enthusiasm when pupils watched Peake's historic arrival at the International Space Station in 2015.

"I remember it like it was yesterday," she said. "I was teaching Year 1 at the time, and the buzz and excitement in the classroom was something I will never forget."

articles.title: Philly officer murdered in line of duty promoted to sergeant as police from around US attend his funeral
articles.summary: Thousands of officers gathered as Shane Seiber was promoted posthumously to sergeant during an emotional Philadelphia funeral service Tuesday.
articles.body: PHILADELPHIA — Thousands of police officers from around the U.S. traveled to the City of Brotherly Love Tuesday for the funeral of Shane Seiber, who was shot and killed in the line of duty on Oct. 10, when prosecutors say an armed suspect shot him and his partner. Philadelphia Police Commissioner Kevin J. Bethel announced during the service at the Cathedral Basilica of Saints Peter and Paul that Seiber had been promoted posthumously to the rank of sergeant. Seiber had served 10 years in the department after spending the prior decade in the Air Force, where he deployed for two tours in Iraq. Officers from around Pennsylvania and other states packed the memorial service to pay their respects. SUSPECT IN DEADLY PHILADELPHIA POLICE AMBUSH FACES 76 CHARGES, ORDERED HELD WITHOUT BAIL Seiber and his partner were responding to a report of a man waving a gun in West Philadelphia when prosecutors say a man named Eric Lewis approached them from behind and asked what they were doing on his doorstep. PHILADELPHIA POLICE OFFICER KILLED, PARTNER SHOT 12 TIMES IN AMBUSH; SUSPECT FOUND HIDING IN TREE They got into an argument, a struggle ensued and then Lewis allegedly opened fire, striking Seiber three times and his partner 12. Lewis was arrested after a standoff with SWAT officers — allegedly carrying two handguns, one belonging to the officers, and a shotgun. FOX 29 Philadelphia has identified Seiber's partner as Officer Hector Rodriguez III, a 33-year-old father of five. He survived his injuries. SEND US A TIP Lewis, 35, had been acquitted at trial in a prior murder case, according to Philadelphia District Attorney Larry Krasner, who blamed a "deeply flawed" investigation. DOJ SENDS GRAND JURY SUBPOENAS TO PHILADELPHIA DA KRASNER AFTER JUDGE'S REFERRAL, SOURCES SAY Philadelphia Mayor Cherelle L. Parker announced that the city would create an annual internship program for public service in Seiber's honor during a eulogy Tuesday, describing him as "a giant of a man" and "clearly a gentleman of the first class." articles.title: 2,000-year-old treasure discovered beneath former sports field, breaking regional record
articles.summary: Archaeologists in Thuringia, Germany, unearthed 11 rare Celtic coins at a construction site. It is the region's largest known hoard from the first century B.C.
articles.body: A trove of ancient coins has been unearthed at a construction site in Germany — after remaining hidden for more than 2,000 years. The discovery, made at Singer Berg in the central German state of Thuringia, was announced recently by the Thuringian State Office for Monument Preservation and Archaeology (TLDA). In a translated news release, officials said excavation director Ronny Krause discovered the coins while archaeologists were investigating a former sports field ahead of the construction of a new fire station. 7,000-YEAR-OLD BONES UNCOVERED AT CONSTRUCTION SITE IN STARTLING FIND Archaeologists conducted follow-up excavations at the site in August 2026 — and confirmed that the 11 coins dated back to the first century B.C. The hoard represented the largest known Celtic coin hoard from that period ever found in Thuringia. The 11 coins, dating back to the first century B.C., were identified as a type of ancient Celtic currency known as Prague-type quinarii. "Until now, only about 80 examples of these quinarii had been identified throughout Thuringia, underscoring the significance of the Singen hoard," the translated statement said. WORKERS RENOVATING MAJOR CITY STREET STUMBLE ON ANCIENT DISCOVERY BURIED 20 FEET BELOW "The mint responsible for producing the coins is believed to have been located in the Gotha region, to the northwest." The Celts were groups of ancient people who lived across much of Europe during the Iron Age, with Celtic languages and traditions surviving today in places such as Ireland, Scotland and Wales. The coins were originally buried together in a container made of organic material that has since decomposed, archaeologists believe. The coins were found scattered across an area measuring roughly 19 feet by 5 feet — likely a result of plowing. Officials described the discovery as a "closed find," suggesting that all the coins originally buried together were recovered. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER While just 11 coins may seem like a modest haul to some, archaeologists consider the discovery a treasure trove of information about the ancient world. "Through the ongoing mapping of discoveries from the same period and cultural background, researchers can draw conclusions about ancient trade routes and production centers," the translated statement added. "The Singen treasure hoard has significantly expanded our existing knowledge in this area." Archaeologists also found an ancient Roman coin and a medieval glass bead — as well as a knife fragment, another silver coin and a Prussian uniform button from the 19th or 20th century. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Officials also emphasized the broader significance of the discovery and the importance of proper archaeological practices. "[The] treasure hoard has significantly expanded our existing knowledge in this area." "This once again demonstrates the importance of preserving the archaeological context of discoveries, in contrast to isolated metal finds recovered, for example, through improper or illegal metal detecting without documentation of their original locations," the statement concluded. Recently, a man using a metal detector in a German field discovered 934 ancient Roman silver coins dating back nearly 2,000 years. articles.title: PHP cyber-security warning sees sites taken down across Europe
articles.summary: Two critical vulnerabilities have been identified with PHP, a programming language which is widely used across the internet.
articles.body:
The Finnish and Dutch governments have taken down websites ahead of a planned software update to a programming language which underpins many online services.

Two critical vulnerabilities with the PHP programming language, which is widely used across the internet, have been identified - a fix is being issued for them on Wednesday afternoon.

Multiple cyber-security agencies have urged organisations to rapidly adopt the updates, or consider taking their websites offline.

Finland has temporarily shut down the government's public web services, while the Netherlands' cyber-security agency says it is taking its own website offline due to the vulnerabilities.

The country's National Institute for Public Health and the Environment, an agency of the Dutch government, has taken down its website.

Similarly the website of the Tweede Kamer, the lower house of the nation's parliament, has become inaccessible.

The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), as well as its counterparts in the EU and Australia have urged those who use PHP to apply the fixes as soon as they become available.

"Where immediate remediation is not feasible, organisations should consider taking the system offline until it can be fully mitigated," the NCSC said in a note .

Japan's national cyber-security office and EU cyber-security officials have issued a similar warning .

"PHP is everywhere. It ​quietly powers WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento sites, shared hosting platforms, control panels, and an awful ⁠lot of software that doesn't even advertise that it runs PHP under the hood," cyber-security company Huntress said.

Cyber-security expert Don Smith, from the Sophos Counter Threat Unit, told the BBC this would "likely be a priority target" for hackers.

The immediate challenge was not simply installing a patch to fix the issue, but finding and managing every instance where PHP was running, he said.

"The use of PHP is pervasive, it can sit beneath public websites, content management systems, hosting platforms and third-party products, sometimes without even being obvious to the organisation using it.

He said it was crucial that organisations looked out for signs that an attacker "might have already have gained a foothold".

The European Union Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-EU) said the risk scores given to the vulnerabilities "indicate the potential for unauthenticated remote code execution".

Such a cyber-attack could potentially allow hackers to install malware and take down websites.

Dane Knecht, chief technology officer at internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare, said he was "seeing early attacks emerging and are updating mitigations as new vectors show up".

The NCSC said once organisations have installed the update, they should "continuously monitor for security updates from third-party software vendors, including for appliances and services that may bundle PHP".

It is not yet clear which versions of the programming language are affected, but CERT-EU said it could affect all versions of it dating back to PHP 5 onwards - which launched in 2004.

PHP was created for web development. It is used on servers to implement what you see when you visit websites.

Not all websites use it, but it nonetheless powers a large portion of the internet.

articles.title: Stranded Iranian tankers, American pressure: Why Sri Lanka faces a difficult choice
articles.summary: Sri Lanka has announced it has no immediate plans to assist 19 Iranian oil tankers anchored in international waters off the island nation's coast, despite
articles.body: Sri Lanka has announced it has no immediate plans to assist 19 Iranian oil tankers anchored in international waters off the island nation's coast, despite shortages of food, water and fuel aboard the vessels.“Sri Lanka will put its national interest first before considering any help, and the companies that supply ships are aware of possible secondary sanctions from the United States,” a foreign ministry spokesperson told reporters in Colombo on October 9.The statement came in response to a Wall Street Journal report earlier this month alleging that US officials had “pressured” Sri Lanka to prevent local shipping firms from supplying the tankers with food and fresh water.However, the foreign ministry spokesperson said the US had not communicated any threat of sanctions if Sri Lanka stepped in to help. Nevertheless, the risk of sanctions appears to be shaping Colombo's response, whether or not Washington has issued a direct warning.Sri Lanka's dilemma is not simply about whether to assist the stranded Iranian vessels, but how far it can act independently when the prospect of US secondary sanctions looms over its decisions.How Iranian ships became stranded near Sri Lanka, and Colombo’s dilemmaOn February 28, the United States and Israel launched joint strikes against Iran, triggering a war in the Middle East. Tehran retaliated with strikes against Israel and targeted American military bases across Gulf states.Iran also blockaded the Strait of Hormuz, a critical sea route, in March, prompting Washington to impose a naval blockade on Iranian ports. The US blockade was later lifted before being reinstated in July. Its resumption left dozens of Iranian vessels stranded off Sri Lanka and neighbouring nations, unable to return home.It was against this backdrop that Sri Lanka said it would prioritise its national interests before assisting the Iranian ships.But where are the ships stranded, and is Colombo legally obliged to assist them?According to Sri Lankan foreign minister Vijitha Herath, around 47 foreign ships are currently anchored off the country's coast, 19 of which are Iranian-flagged. Herath said all the vessels are stranded within Sri Lanka's Exclusive Economic Zone but outside the 12-nautical-mile limit of its territorial waters.This creates a dilemma for Sri Lanka. Article 98 of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) requires states to promote effective search-and-rescue services and ships to assist people in distress at sea. However, the extent of Colombo's legal obligation to provide supplies depends on whether the sailors are in distress and the circumstances of their requests for assistance, rather than simply the vessels' location outside territorial waters.We haven’t provided them (Iranian vessels) with anything so far, and we don’t intend to do so in the future either. ... Such supplies to vessels are usually provided by the private sector, and this is a matter for them.Dayan Jayatilleka, Sri Lanka's former Permanent Representative to the UN, acknowledged that Colombo was in a “difficult situation.”“We are caught in a difficult situation. It's clear to the world that we are not willingly refusing to assist, but there are reasons we have to be careful and to deliberate,” The Associated Press quoted Jayatilleka as saying.Sri Lanka's hesitation, therefore, appears to stem not from an unwillingness to help, but from the position it finds itself in: provide assistance and risk possible US action, or withhold it and leave the seafarers to their fate.How US uses secondary sanctions to pressure governmentsSecondary sanctions are imposed by a government on third parties to maintain or intensify pressure on a primary sanctions target. Although the sanctioning government cannot directly compel foreign entities to comply with its policies, it can restrict its own companies and citizens from doing business with the third party. This puts the designated firm under severe pressure to sever its commercial ties with the primary target.Leveraging the dollar's central role in global finance, Washington uses secondary sanctions to discourage countries and foreign businesses from maintaining commercial ties with Iran or entities linked to Tehran. Although not legally bound by US sanctions in all cases, many comply to avoid losing access to the US financial system.This is where the secondary sanctions threat hits home for Sri Lanka, and the Iranian tankers are caught in the crossfire because of Operation Economic Outcast, the latest in a decades-long series of US sanctions against Iran.Announced on August 24, Operation Economic Outcast expanded the risk of secondary sanctions for foreign individuals and entities doing business with Tehran, including in the shipping sector.With so much at stake, a Sri Lankan shipping company may therefore conclude that the risks of assisting the Iranian tankers are too severe to justify providing them with services.Sri Lanka’s maritime industry: What is at stakeSri Lanka lies in the Indian Ocean, making it a key maritime hub. However, this strategic location also makes its shipping industry dependent on international trade and vulnerable to disruptions caused by geopolitical tensions and sanctions.The maritime sector, which includes shipping and other sea-related activities, has historically contributed around 2.5% of Sri Lanka's GDP. It provides full-time, direct employment to approximately 40,000–50,000 people. Around 70% of service providers are Sri Lankan-owned, while the remainder are multinational companies. Sri Lanka is also home to 130 shipping agencies.The presence of these agencies reflects Sri Lanka's integration into international shipping networks. Maintaining these connections is important if Colombo wants to expand its maritime sector and increase its contribution to the national economy. However, the threat of US secondary sanctions could complicate companies' decisions on whether to provide services to Iranian-flagged vessels, potentially putting Sri Lanka's maritime ambitions at odds with the risks of doing business with entities linked to Tehran.With its maritime industry growing, the question for Sri Lanka is whether it can assist Iranian vessels while managing the risk of US secondary sanctions.We have informed the private sector that they should be extremely careful and act responsibly. Otherwise, they run the risk of falling foul of US sanctionsWhy Sri Lanka can't defy USThe threat of secondary sanctions is not specific to Sri Lankan companies; any non-US entity doing business with Iran could face similar risks. However, there is a significant asymmetry between Sri Lanka and larger, wealthier economies in their ability to absorb the economic consequences of a confrontation with Washington.For instance, in 2025, Sri Lankan companies exported goods worth $2,999 million to the United States, while importing $544 million worth of goods in return. While this trade surplus benefits Sri Lanka in some ways, it also highlights the asymmetry between the two countries: the US accounted for around 24% of Sri Lanka’s total exports that year, whereas Sri Lanka represents a relatively small market for American exports.(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(`message`,function(e){if(e.data[`datawrapper-height`]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(`iframe`);for(var n in e.data[`datawrapper-height`])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[`datawrapper-height`][n]+`px`;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();Therefore, with nearly a quarter of its exports going to the US alone, Sri Lanka has a significant economic stake in maintaining access to the American market. Any disruption could affect exporters, businesses and workers who depend on it. This makes the potential costs of antagonising the Trump administration difficult for Colombo to ignore, even in the absence of a direct threat from Washington.(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(`message`,function(e){if(e.data[`datawrapper-height`]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(`iframe`);for(var n in e.data[`datawrapper-height`])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[`datawrapper-height`][n]+`px`;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();There is also the added context of the 2022 economic crisis, Sri Lanka’s worst since its independence in 1948. The United States provided economic and humanitarian assistance during the economic crisis and reportedly supported Colombo’s efforts to secure a four-year, $3 billion IMF bailout programme, approved in March 2023.This imbalance gives Washington further leverage over Colombo, narrowing Sri Lanka’s room for manoeuvre.What can Sri Lanka doHowever, Sri Lanka has not always aligned itself with the US. In recent months, Colombo has taken decisions that diverged from Washington's preferences, reflecting its efforts to preserve strategic autonomy while balancing relations with competing powers.President Anura Kumara Dissanayake revealed on March 20 that his government had rejected a US request to allow two American combat aircraft to land at a civilian airport in southern Sri Lanka. According to Dissanayake, Washington made the request on February 26, two days before the Iran war began.Before that, on March 5, the Sri Lankan Navy rescued 206 sailors from the Iranian warship IRIS Bushehr after one of its engines malfunctioned and the vessel requested assistance. In total, Sri Lanka rescued 238 sailors, including 32 crew members from IRIS Dena, another Iranian warship that was sunk by a US Navy torpedo attack on March 4, four days after the Iran war began.Jayatilleka, the former Sri Lankan diplomat, highlighted that the stranded vessels are cargo ships, not warships, and argued that Sri Lanka has a moral obligation to render assistance.“These are cargo ships which carried oil to China from Iran. If these ships come in for some reason to our waters because they are attacked, we have a moral obligation to assist immediately,” he said.Colombo's past decisions show that it can exercise strategic autonomy. Whether it can do so again is another question.Limits of Sri Lanka’s strategic autonomyAlthough the Sri Lankan government has repeatedly maintained that its decisions are not influenced by US pressure, its position over the Iranian tankers raises questions about the limits of strategic autonomy in an unequal international system.Also, the fact that Colombo has acted independently in the past does not mean it can do so again without risking economic repercussions from Washington, which could be particularly damaging for a country still recovering from a severe economic crisis.Sri Lanka's final decision will therefore not only affect its relationship with the US or Iran, depending on what it does, but will also test its commitment to humanitarian principles. It will also determine how far Colombo can pursue an independent foreign policy without jeopardising its economic interests.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Iran’s enriched uranium re-emerges as point of contention in US talks
articles.summary: Iran’s nuclear enrichment has emerged as a major point of contention amid diplomatic push to end the war.
articles.body:
The renewed diplomatic push to end the United States-Israel war on Iran is facing headwinds as Tehran’s nuclear programme, which the two countries invoked to launch the war in February, has once again emerged as one of the biggest stumbling blocks in reaching a ceasefire.

Nearly eight months into the war, which has caused a global energy crisis, a deal to ensure a permanent ceasefire remains elusive. Moreover, the war has since spilled into a regional conflict, with Yemen emerging as its latest theatre.

The reopening of the Strait of Hormuz – a global oil chokepoint – was the focus of the June Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) signed between the US and Iran.

The MoU had also stated that Iran “shall not procure or develop nuclear weapons”, but a comprehensive deal, including the nuclear issue, could not be thrashed out within the stipulated 60-day period. Analysts said that differing interpretations of the agreement clauses caused the MoU to fall apart.

Now the nuclear issue has once again emerged as the central point of contention, with Tehran insisting that uranium enrichment is a right guaranteed under the Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT).

US President Donald Trump, on the other hand, has called for “zero uranium enrichment”. His ally, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, on Sunday reiterated his pledge to topple the Iranian government, which he said is key to preventing it from developing nuclear weapons.

Earlier this week, US Vice President JD Vance appeared to offer concessions on the nuclear doctrine to reach a deal.

While Qatar and Pakistan are engaged in mediation efforts, how will they get the sides to agree on the nuclear enrichment issue?

Pakistan’s army chief Asim Munir, who is also a key negotiator in the conflict, is currently in Tehran, where he met Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei on Tuesday.

In the meeting, Rezaei said “even a particle of enriched uranium will not exit Iran at all,” according to comments carried by Iran’s semi-official Fars news agency, describing the material as a major national asset that would remain in the country for domestic use.

His response came amid media reports that the US wants Iran to transfer part of its enriched uranium out of the country. Trump has previously called for the removal of the enriched uranium stockpile from Iran.

Rezaei also said negotiations with the US would not begin until Washington fulfils trust-building measures, including meeting the latest conditions Iran has set.

Iran wants the US to lift its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waive sanctions, and release frozen Iranian assets as part of its latest terms to end the war. In return, Iran has promised to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

Another Iranian lawmaker, Alaeddin Boroujerdi, also a member of the Iranian parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, reiterated that Iran is not seeking the production of nuclear weapons.

“Iran’s enrichment activities are unrelated to the US, and Washington should focus on fulfilling its own obligations regarding nuclear arms reduction,” he said.

Addressing a Republican Party campaign rally earlier this week, Trump claimed that the US bombing had destroyed Iran’s nuclear facilities and that he would not allow Tehran to rebuild them.

“They cannot have a nuclear weapon,” Trump told his supporters at a rally at Northern Kentucky University.

Vice President Vance said earlier this week that the US has “in some ways decisively won” the war on Iran and has destroyed the country’s nuclear programme.

He told a town hall hosted by CBS News that the US was now focused on ensuring that Iran makes a “long-term” and “verifiable commitment” not to rebuild its nuclear programme.

“Not over the administration of Donald Trump … but five years from now, could the Iranians rebuild that nuclear arsenal? Could they try to rebuild that enrichment capacity?” he asked.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio also said this week that a decision to end the war finally rests with Trump. “The US will not support any deal that creates a pathway for Iran to have a nuclear weapon. As long as President Trump is in office, they will not have a nuclear weapon,” he reiterated.

Last month, Vance told the Reuters news agency in an interview that Tehran must make a “meaningful” reduction in its nuclear enrichment capacity to satisfy US demands and end the war.

“If you don’t want a nuclear weapon, then why do you need 60 percent enriched fuel? And if you want to show commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, don’t build highly enriched fuel. That’s a very basic threshold issue,” Vance said.

“I think if they want to show a commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, they would do something meaningful on their enrichment capacity,” he added.

What the MoU says about Iran’s uranium programme

The MoU signed on June 17 left the future of Iran’s enriched uranium stockpile to further negotiations, but identified downblending under international supervision of the International Atomic Energy Agency as the minimum approach to resolving the issue.

Downblending involves mixing highly enriched uranium with lower-enriched material, making it less suitable for rapid conversion into weapons-grade material.

The MoU left room for Iran to reduce the material’s enrichment domestically rather than surrender it. However, it did not specify the quantity to be downblended, a target enrichment level or a detailed implementation timetable.

“The two parties also agreed to discuss the issue of enrichment and other mutually agreed matters related to the Islamic Republic of Iran’s nuclear needs, based on a satisfactory framework being agreed upon in the final deal,” the MoU clause reads.

That final deal, of course, could not be reached as the MoU expired in mid-August.

The Trump administration invoked the imminent threat of Iran acquiring nuclear weapons to launch the war on February 28, 2026. On the first day of the war, US-Israel strikes killed Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who had banned the development of nuclear weapons in a fatwa, or religious edict.

President Trump has often argued that Iran would use the nuclear weapon “within moments after getting it”, and then “the Middle East would be gone, Israel would be gone, and then hit Europe probably next.”

The US president has spoken out against Iran’s nuclear programme numerous times in the past.

As the war progressed over months, the US focus shifted gradually towards reopening the Strait of Hormuz as a base condition of the ongoing fighting.

Speaking in Alaska last week, Trump again falsely claimed that he had to start his war on Iran because, “[Iran was] two weeks away from having a nuclear weapon.”

In April, Trump had warned that “the enriched material, sometimes referred to as ‘Nuclear Dust,’ will be unearthed by the United States … and DESTROYED.” Later in the month, he told reporters on board Air Force One that the US would “go in with Iran, and we will take it together, and we will bring it back. 100 percent of it back to the United States.”

Mostafa Najafi, a foreign policy analyst based in Iran, noted that “despite [the US’s] insistence on nuclear negotiations and obtaining tangible concessions in this area, [Washington is] unwilling to offer significant concessions such as lifting sanctions.”

The US wants “to secure major concessions solely in exchange for lifting the blockade and releasing some of Iran’s assets”, he wrote in a post on X. “From Iran’s perspective, lifting the blockade and releasing assets is no longer a noteworthy concession for Tehran!”
