articles.title: ‘They try to break us’: Pro-Palestine activists in Czech custody
articles.summary: As a group is accused of an attack on a weapons factory, activists allege growing crackdown on the solidarity movement.
articles.body:
Prague, Czech Republic – Youssef Moursi, a 25-year-old Egyptian university student and activist in Prague, has spent the last six months in pre-trial detention, accused of an arson attack in March against a Czech weapons factory with alleged ties to Israel.

Moursi is one of 11 people being charged with “terrorism” for the attack and could face up to 20 years in prison if convicted.

The case has echoes of legal battles in the United Kingdom , where Palestine Action activists have been sentenced under terrorism laws, and Germany , where five people accused of targeting a site linked to Elbit Systems, Israel’s largest weapons maker, are on trial.

Moursi, a humanities student at Charles University, said in a statement to Al Jazeera that “a group of armed and masked policemen smashed down [my] front door”, two days after the alleged attack, in which he denies any involvement.

He spent the first three months of his detention in solitary confinement, according to his lawyer. Today, he is allowed one hour outside his cell and 20 minutes on the phone a day, with visits from friends and family every two weeks.

“[There] is the psychological front being waged against us, where [the police] deliberately try to break us by putting some of us in solitary confinement for months, denying us visits, blocking correspondence, or spreading fear,” Moursi said. “Putting people in custody and prolonging it time and time again without direct evidence, mainly based on a mix of inclinations, activism, racism, and an attempted blurring of freedom of speech, is unacceptable.”

Moursi and his lawyer, Pavel Cizinsky, believe he has been targeted because of his involvement in pro-Palestine activism in Prague.

Cizinsky said part of the evidence police have against Moursi is that on the day after the fire, he posted advice for pro-Palestinian activists on social media, should they be approached by officers. Cizinsky called this “ridiculous.”

“If you put into Google what to do when interviewed by the police, the first advice is wait for your lawyer. But if you say it as a pro-Palestinian activist, if you write it to your friends, then it’s reason against you that you are guilty,” Cizinsky said.

At the beginning of the investigation, Cizinsky said he faced pressure from the authorities not to take the case. As a result, he was not present during the initial interrogation and house raid on Moursi’s flat.

“It is clear that there is extraordinary attention to this investigation by the police, and really great resources dedicated to this case,” Cizinsky said. “But the fact that he is already five months in prison is surely a breach of law.”

Under Czech law, individuals held in pre-trial detention who have not been convicted must have their detention reviewed by a court every three months. Moursi’s detention has so far been reviewed twice, with the court deciding each time that he must stay in prison.

His detention will be reviewed again in early December, and the trial is expected to start within a year.

The fire broke out in the early hours of March 20 at LPP Holding, a Czech weapons factory in Pardubice, about 120km (75 miles) east of Prague.

No one was injured but police said the building was destroyed, with damage estimates reaching hundreds of millions of crowns, or at least four million euros.

A previously unknown pro-Palestinian group called The Earthquake Faction claimed responsibility and posted videos of the fire, saying it targeted LPP Holding for its cooperation with Elbit Systems, an Israeli weapons company.

In 2023, LPP Holding and Elbit Systems announced a partnership to build drones in the Czech Republic. But on the day of the fire, an LPP Holding spokesperson told Czech media the collaboration never happened.

In the weeks following the attack, police launched a manhunt and arrested several foreign nationals including Ukrainian, Czech, Slovak, Polish and American citizens. Of the 10 other individuals accused, three are under house arrest in Poland and seven remain behind bars in the Czech Republic.

Over the past two years, Elbit Systems has become a primary target for pro-Palestine activists across Europe.

In June, a UK court convicted four imprisoned Palestine Action members of criminal damage with a “terrorist connection” after a raid on an Elbit Systems factory in Filton, near Bristol. In September last year, police in Poland arrested protesters at an arms fair for throwing red liquid over an Elbit Systems stand. This week, an elderly man in Germany was arrested after protesting against the Israeli weapons giant.

In Prague, the atmosphere for pro-Palestinian activists has grown increasingly tense.

A collective called Prague 4 Palestine Youth stopped organising demonstrations and charity events after police investigations into dozens of its members in the months following the arson attack.

Rue, a 25-year-old Czech activist who requested anonymity, said that friends of those detained in the arson case and fellow activists are being subjected to interrogations, house raids, and indefinite confiscations of their devices as the investigation continues.

Nine days after the fire, Rue said, “[The police] interrogated us, and then they took us back to [our] apartment where they did a search of the house. They kept us awake for more than 24 hours. I was having panic attacks for a week straight after it happened.”

After the interrogation and house search, Rue was told they were being treated as a witness to the arson attack. The police confiscated their phone and computer, which have not been returned.

Rue believes they were investigated because of their friendship with suspects in the arson case. They have visited two in prison; one is in solitary confinement for 23 hours a day, Rue said.

“When it comes to the end of the visit, the tears come,” Rue added. “You’re free to go anywhere and do anything, and they go back to being in those four walls.”

The individuals detained in the Czech Republic could remain in prison for up to four years without being convicted, according to their lawyers.

Police confirmed they have arrested and charged suspects of several different nationalities and remanded them in custody.

“Given the gravity of the case and the ongoing investigation into terrorism-related offences, the supervising public prosecutor’s office has assumed exclusive authority to release information,” the police said.

articles.title: Off-duty Con Ed worker killed in GWB apparent road rage shooting
articles.summary: A gunman was still wanted by police Wednesday morning, hours after killing another driver in what police suspect was a case of road rage on the George Washington Bridge.
articles.body: A gunman was still wanted by police Wednesday morning, hours after killing another driver in what police suspect was a case of road rage on the George Washington Bridge. Law enforcement sources said a 46-year-old off-duty Con Edison worker was gunned down Tuesday night when the gunman fired a shot through a window of the man’s car, striking him in the shoulder. The shooting shut down the bridge around 7 p.m. According to sources, the victim was captured on video nearly crashing his blue Volkswagen Golf into another driver an entrance ramp to the GWB. Shortly after, the 46-year-old’s rear passenger window was shot out with what law enforcement sources believe was a lone gunshot. The bullet appeared to strike the driver’s seat headrest before entering the driver’s body, law enforcement sources told News 4. The victim’s car later struck a median, bringing it to a full stop. The suspect was seen driving on. Late Tuesday, investigators said the incident was potentially the result of a road rage dispute. The NYPD has not released any description of the suspected shooter. Authorities remained on scene through much of the night canvassing the area for ballistics and have been reviewing surveillance cameras for more information about the other car involved. All lanes of the bridge were reopened around 1 a.m. The identity of the victim has been withheld as police work to identify the man’s family.

articles.title: Trump’s Russian roulette: A high-stakes juggle between Vladimir Putin and the polls
articles.summary: With US fuel prices soaring weeks before the midterm elections, US President Donald Trump turned to a most unlikely supplier for relief. Russia.
articles.body: With US fuel prices soaring weeks before the midterm elections, US President Donald Trump turned to a most unlikely supplier for relief. Russia. Moscow, which Washington has sanctioned for years over its war in Ukraine, is now being allowed to supply diesel to the US and global markets under a temporary licence issued by the Treasury Department.The decision came after a telephone conversation between Trump and his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin. The White House said the move will help bring down fuel costs for American farmers, truckers and families. But critics, including several Republicans, argue that the deal risks putting money into Moscow's hands while doing little to ease prices for American consumers.The timing is politically sensitive as Americans are preparing to elect a new Congress on November 3, and the cost of living remains a major concern.For Trump, the political calculation appears straightforward. If Russian supplies arrive quickly and in sufficient quantities, they could help ease fuel prices and give his party a political boost. If deliveries fall short or prices remain high, the administration could end up granting Moscow significant economic relief without delivering much for American consumers.How much difference can Russian diesel make?Diesel prices averaged $6.28 a gallon on October 11, up 71% from a year earlier. The American Automobile Association (AAA), which tracks fuel prices, put the average at $6.33 on October 16.The impact extends well beyond motorists because diesel also powers the lorries that transport goods, tractors used by farmers and cargo vessels that move products around the world. When diesel becomes more expensive, the cost of transporting food and other essentials rises, eventually feeding into household bills.Farm-state Republicans had pressed the White House to act, with Senator Chuck Grassley of Iowa and others calling for a ban on fuel exports to protect domestic supplies. Trump initially backed the idea, but the White House later ruled it out. The administration subsequently turned to Russian diesel.In announcing the deal, Trump said bringing down prices for American farmers, ranchers and truckers was his highest priority.According to Trump's announcement, Russia would supply approximately 2.24 million barrels immediately, followed by 3.73 million barrels the next month, with subsequent supplies expected to roughly double.Russia said on October 21 that it would send its first diesel shipment to the US the following day, carrying 40,000 metric tonnes of fuel. More shipments are planned, although questions remain over whether Moscow can deliver enough diesel to make a significant difference to prices.The figures, however, offer a sense of the deal's limitations. The second shipment, spread over a month, would amount to around 124,000 barrels a day. Kpler, a market intelligence firm, estimates the global diesel shortfall at about one million barrels a day. The planned shipment would therefore cover only around one-eighth of that gap.And there is also no guarantee that Russia can deliver the promised volumes. The International Energy Agency has said Russian diesel production has fallen by about 30 per cent, with Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries contributing to the squeeze.Rachel Ziemba, an analyst specialising in economics and geopolitics, said the measure was unlikely to make a significant difference to the global diesel market in the near term. Kpler's Michelle Brouhard has also warned that Russia's ability to supply additional barrels remains uncertain.Even if Russian diesel reaches the market, lower wholesale prices may not immediately translate into cheaper fuel for Americans. Refining capacity, transportation costs and the time required for deliveries could affect how quickly consumers see any relief.A lifeline for MoscowWhile the benefit to American consumers is still unclear, the decision could offer Russia a more immediate advantage by opening a route to sell fuel that sanctions had restricted.The Treasury licence remains valid until April 7, 2027, making it significantly longer than the usual 30-day sanctions waivers. It is the first diesel waiver since the start of the Ukraine war to extend beyond that standard period.Putin had said days before the announcement that Russia had ample diesel supplies but was struggling to sell them abroad because of sanctions. News agency Reuters reported that his envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, had visited Washington the previous month seeking licences covering major Russian oil companies.Dmitriev welcomed the Treasury notice, saying Russian-American cooperation on diesel and energy would benefit the world. He later described the broader sanctions waiver as a historic moment.The move was followed by a broader sanctions waiver. On October 16, Trump signed an executive order waiving sanctions and tariffs provided for under the newly enacted Graham Act, certifying that the decision was in the national interest.The waiver suspended new sanctions and potential tariffs under the law, including penalties targeting countries that purchase Russian energy. India and China were among the countries that could have faced additional trade restrictions. The White House argued that enforcing the measures would obstruct efforts to negotiate an end to the war.Together, the decisions marked a sharp shift from Trump's earlier approach. Last year, his administration imposed an additional 25% tariff on India over its purchases of Russian oil. On October 2, Trump and other G7 leaders had also pledged to maintain pressure on Moscow.A bipartisan group of US senators has since warned that easing restrictions would not serve American interests and would help finance Russia's war against Ukraine.Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who learnt about the diesel deal after it had been finalised, called it unfair and dishonest, describing it as a sign of weakness. Trump responded by suggesting that Ukraine needed a new president and later said Putin appeared more interested in reaching a deal than Zelenskyy.Trump has also placed the burden on Ukraine to end the nearly four-year war with Russia, arguing that Moscow's military strength and territorial gains leave Kyiv at a disadvantage."Ukraine has to want to settle this war," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office, signalling that he expects Kyiv to move towards a negotiated settlement even as the fighting continues.Trump pointed to Russia's ability to sustain its military campaign and capture territory, portraying Moscow as having the upper hand in the conflict."Russia is a big machine - they just keep grinding forward, and that's what they've done. They've taken a very large piece of land," he said.Trump also questioned the value of American assistance to Kyiv, complaining that Washington had spent heavily on supporting Ukraine without receiving anything in return."We've given a lot to Ukraine. We've gotten absolutely nothing back except grief, death, tremendous monetary loss," he said.The US administration has defended its decision by pointing to Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, which it says have contributed to higher fuel prices. A US official told Axios that Trump acted after Zelenskyy ignored repeated requests to stop the strikes.However, Russia has continued attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure despite an energy ceasefire announced by Trump, with no comparable punitive action from Washington.Republicans divided as election pressure mountsThe backlash has exposed divisions within Trump's own party. Republican senators Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, Mitch McConnell, John Cornyn and Thom Tillis joined Democrats in criticising the deal, calling it a betrayal of Ukraine and a gift to an adversary.Congressman Brian Fitzpatrick has vowed to force a House vote to block the purchases, predicting overwhelming support for the measure. Senator Richard Blumenthal, a co-sponsor of the sanctions legislation, has also condemned the administration's decision.Other Republicans, including Anna Paulina Luna and Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso, have defended it. White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said the deal would help farmers, truckers and families while Trump continued pressing both sides to stop attacks on refineries.The decision has also raised legal questions. Seven senators argue that allowing Russian petroleum products into the US violates a 2022 law barring such imports. Tillis has separately questioned whether the administration complied with requirements to notify Congress before lifting sanctions. The Treasury Department maintains that its actions comply with applicable laws.For European governments, the easing of pressure on Moscow is particularly uncomfortable as Nato allies contend with Russian sabotage, cyberattacks and drone incursions. Zelenskyy has warned that Russia could repay the concession with further attacks and deception.Domestic politics help explain why Trump is keen to show results quickly. A Pew Research Center poll found that 44% of registered voters viewed their congressional vote as a way to oppose Trump, compared with 19% who saw it as a way to support him.Trump has urged Republicans to campaign as though he were on the ballot, even as he insists that his own electoral victories are already settled.The Russian diesel deal is therefore more than an energy decision. It is an attempt to address a pressing economic problem while navigating an election, a costly war and competing demands from allies.With the November 3 election approaching, the central question is whether the promised fuel will reach the market in sufficient quantities to make a noticeable difference. For now, Washington has opened the door to Russian diesel, but whether the decision brings relief to American consumers remains uncertain.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Who is Stephen Hubbard, the retired American teacher freed by Russia?
articles.summary: Stephen James Hubbard, a retired American teacher, was released by Russia on Wednesday after nearly five years in detention in the midst of an apparent warming of ties between Washington and Moscow.
articles.body: Stephen James Hubbard, a retired American teacher, was released by Russia on Wednesday after nearly five years in detention in the midst of an apparent warming of ties between Washington and Moscow. The 74-year-old from Michigan had been living in eastern Ukraine for years when Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022. He was detained two months into the war as Russia captured swaths of Ukrainian territory. Two years later, he was convicted by a Russian court of serving as a mercenary. The news of his release came out of a meeting between President Donald Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff and Russian President Vladimir Putin on Wednesday, where they were due to discuss an end to the Ukraine war. Witkoff thanked Putin for freeing Hubbard during their on-camera talks. Putin’s foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov later said Hubbard was handed over to Witkoff at St. Petersburg’s Pulkovo airport. In a video from Russian state news agency Ria, Hubbard can be seen wearing a green jacket and smiling as he met Witkoff. “Thank you very much for all your efforts,” the freed American tells Witkoff as they shake hands. Putin sent Hubbard “blessings,” Witkoff tells him, adding “from today, it’s a new life.” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Putin released Hubbard “on humanitarian grounds,” though Russia did not provide more details. Hubbard’s family acknowledged both Trump’s and Putin’s roles in securing his release. “We have been gravely concerned for his safety and health since his 2022 detention,” Hubbard’s son, the Rev. Joseph Coleman, who is an Orthodox priest, said in a statement on behalf of the family. “Never once did we waver as we prayed for success in these negotiations, and we must acknowledge that this humanitarian move by President Putin in this matter is deeply appreciated,” the statement said. Martin De Luca, Hubbard’s lawyer, said in a separate statement that his client was the only American in Russia currently designated by the U.S. government as wrongfully detained. His firm appealed for privacy “as Stephen recovers and reconnects with the people who love him.” “Stephen is on his way back home and will soon be with his family,” Trump said in a post on Truth Social on Wednesday, shortly after Witkoff announced Hubbard’s release. “The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return — an unprecedented situation for Russia.” There was no “swap” necessary for this release, Trump added, though in a later post he said “those negotiations would have come to a complete and total halt” had the U.S. gone ahead with sanctions that he waived last week. Hubbard was sentenced in a closed-door trial in 2024, with very little information about his case reported by Russian state media. At the time, Russian prosecutors alleged that as the Kremlin launched its “special military operation” in Ukraine in February 2022, Hubbard voluntarily joined a territorial defense battalion in the eastern city of Izyum, where he had been living since 2014. The prosecutors said Hubbard took part in the war in Ukraine and regularly received financial compensation before his detention in April 2022 as advancing Russian forces captured the city. “He was aware of the unlawful nature of his actions, yet — with the deliberate intent of personal enrichment — he carried out the orders of his superiors, which entailed direct participation in combat operations on the side of the Armed Forces of Ukraine against service members of the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation,” according to Russia’s prosecutor general’s office. Russian state media reported he pleaded guilty to the charges. ​But De Luca previously told Reuters that Hubbard had told him the ​charges against him were false and ​that ⁠he was not in any combat or military unit. The New York Times reported last year that Patricia Hubbard Fox, Hubbard’s sister, disputes that he fought for Ukraine, as do three former Ukrainian prisoners of war held with Hubbard. The paper also cited Fox as saying that her brother had a master’s degree in English, and had lived in Japan and Cyprus before moving to eastern Ukraine, where he had a Ukrainian partner. Fox also said that Hubbard taught English online when he needed money, and did not speak either Ukrainian or Russian. Izyum, where Fox said her brother settled, was occupied by Russia for six months in 2022, but was later recaptured by Ukraine in a major counteroffensive. It is currently held by Ukraine and is not part of the four Ukrainian oblasts Russia has illegally annexed. Hubbard’s release from Russian custody comes just months after former U.S. Marine Robert Gilman, who spent more than four years in a Russian prison, was set free in August. Washington has accused Moscow of arbitrarily detaining American citizens in Russia for years, with their cases often used to negotiate prisoner swaps, including for state-backed intelligence operatives, detained around the world. In some of the more high-profile cases, U.S. journalist Evan Gershkovich was released in a swap in 2024, alongside Marine veteran Paul Whelan — both had been jailed on espionage charges. WNBA star Brittney Griner, detained on drug charges in 2022, was freed after the Biden administration negotiated her release in exchange for a Russian arms dealer.

articles.title: From one house to villages: Israeli settlers have Palestinians surrounded
articles.summary: A family in the South Hebron Hills has spent more than two weeks cut off by settlers camped outside.
articles.body:
Yousef Shanaran, 52, built a well beside his house, which he can no longer reach. Since October 5, Israeli settlers have besieged his family home in Wadi Rakhim around the clock, a once-quiet corner of the South Hebron Hills among limestone rocks and thorny brush. They are unable to go outside on their own, even to fetch a little water from the well.

It took five days for the army to coordinate the family’s access to the well. After running out of water three days earlier, the Israeli army on Tuesday allowed them to retrieve some from the well.

“Food, there’s none,” Shanaran, who built the sturdy two-storey house in 2016 on land between the Palestinian town of as-Samu and the village of Susiya, planting about 70 grapevines and 30 to 40 olive trees, told Al Jazeera by phone.

“My well, full of water; I built it and lost money on it,” he said. “They keep me from it because they want to get me out of my house.”

More than half a year ago, settlers pitched a tent 300 metres (about 1,000 feet) from the Shanaran residence, restricting the family’s movement and exposing them to attacks and intimidation. On October 5, the tent was moved just 30 metres from their home. That day, about 50 settlers attacked the family with sticks and pepper spray. This marked the beginning of the full siege on Shanaran’s home.

Nasser Nawajeh, a longtime B’Tselem field researcher who now heads the Susiya village council in Masafer Yatta, has tried to deliver supplies to the Shanaran family during the siege, but most attempts have failed. “Once I tried to bring aid to the people, and right away there was an attack from the settlers,” he told Al Jazeera. “I mean they’re there 24 hours to attack.”

Nothing can move in or out of Shanaran’s home without the army’s permission. “This is a displacement policy,” he said. “If they want to take the kids out to school, we have to wait for the army to take them. If you want to bring in food or water, we have to do coordination.”

Since October 15, he has kept asking the army for coordination to deliver supplies to the family — and given excuses each day: “‘The army’s busy, can’t come, there aren’t any forces’ — they tell us ‘tomorrow and tomorrow’,” he said.

There are now two armies to contend with, Nawajeh said: the settlers’ regional units, the Kitat Konenut, meaning rapid response squads in Hebrew; and the regular army, which “comes, demolishes [the settlers’ tent] and leaves”. When the soldiers leave, the settlers simply pitch up their tent again.

Shanaran said the soldiers stationed outside his house do nothing. “They stand and sit, eating and drinking, relaxed, at the door of the house,” he said.

Nawajeh said the soldiers’ presence essentially amounts to a green light for the siege to continue.

“Sometimes the soldiers don’t even stop the settlers coming close; they hit people and sit with the soldiers at the door,” he said. As the house is in Area B, an area technically under joint Israeli-Palestinian control, the army could arrest all the settlers as there is a closure order against them. “But there’s no enforcement of these laws,” he added.

The soldiers posted outside the family home see their ostensible job as shielding the family from a beating, not ending the blockade. “In practice, the Palestinians are living in a prison inside. The siege is basically a prison,” he added.

Shanaran said his family, trapped in their home, is living a life worse than prison.

“Prison ends. Here, you’re sitting in your own house, and they’ve locked you up in it — and you’re afraid,” he said.

‘If they drive out the first house, they drive out the second’

The Shanaran home is the closest Palestinian one to the outposts encroaching on it, Nawajeh said. Settlers see no difference between Area A, intended to be administered by Palestinians, Area B under mixed Israeli-Palestinian authority, and Area C, which is fully under Israeli military and civil control.

“They start with the house on the edge, in the corner. If they drive out the first house, they drive out the second,” he added.

This tactic is now being applied in Masafer Yatta, an area south of the occupied West Bank which has come under repeated Israeli settler and military attacks.

Following similar sieges further north in Jalud, where the Tubasi family was forced from their home in July and attacked in September when they tried to return under a court order, and in Qusra, where settlers besieged three homes , one owned by an American citizen, before the army set up barracks beside the besieged homes.

B’Tselem’s Yair Dvir believes that the fact that the Qusra siege drew wide coverage was because one of the Palestinians involved held US citizenship.

“In reality, attacks like these occur continually across the West Bank,” Dvir said.

Settlers have now built more than 400 outposts across the West Bank, isolating Palestinian homes and communities through their control of nearby hilltops and pathways.

Dror Etkes, cofounder of the settlement-monitoring group Kerem Navot, said, with Palestinians surrounded, these doorstep sieges reflect “an advanced stage of the complete collapse of any rule of law, any attempt to enforce law in the West Bank”.

Violence that once kept Palestinians off open grazing and farmland is gradually moving into built-up areas, Etkes said. Driving whole farming communities off their land in one fell swoop is still beyond settlers’ reach, he said, but “what they’re trying to do right now is to expel certain families … who are residing outside of the big cluster of a built-up area”.

Ateret settlement from Umm Safa landsAt the eastern end of the farming village of Umm Safa, northwest of Ramallah, stands the home of Muhammad al-Abayat. The family has lived there since 1973, before the nearby illegal settlement of Ateret was established, according to the village mayor, Marwan Sabah. It now sits between Ateret and one of the six outposts surrounding the village.

Late in September, Israeli settlers pitched a tent at the family’s door, then fixed a gate blocking the path to their home, where 15 people live. The children cannot get to school, and al-Abayat’s wife is ill and needs an operation.

“Even his kids are banned; the family can barely get the basic supplies to him,” Sabah said. Anyone who tries to reach the family is attacked or pepper-sprayed. The village won a court ruling and a police decision to open the gate, but “the settlers lock the gate themselves most of the time”, he said.

The mayor says the village as a whole faces a “suffocating siege”, with illegal outposts surrounding it and military support buttressing them. “Right now all of Umm Safa’s land is under the settlers’ control, including the village cemetery,” he said. Now that the harvest is under way, “all the olives are in their hands”.

Even basic services are becoming impossible, “all the rubbish — we can’t get it out”, he added.

Amid the settler siege on October 20, the Israeli Civil Administration issued a demolition notice for the Abayat family home.

In Madama, south of Nablus, settler outposts in Area B to the north and west, along with an illegal settlement and bypass road to the south, have surrounded the village. On October 12, the army sealed all three main entrances to the village with earth mounds. On the same day, a weeklong siege of neighbouring Burin was lifted.

This forced villagers, including teachers, women and children, to quickly cross the mounds on foot while two cars waited on either side, said Wail Qut, a Madama resident and lawyer with the Jerusalem Legal Aid and Human Rights Center (JLAC), which is challenging a new Area B outpost near the village before Israel’s High Court. A teacher was beaten by settlers while trying to cross, he said, and two dialysis patients now face a far longer route to the hospital where they need regular treatment.

On October 18, a bulldozer that villagers say came from the Yitzhar illegal settlement shut the last road in use – a backroad towards Asira al-Qibliya, uprooting nearby olive trees. According to Qut, the army’s District Coordination Office told the mayor the barriers would stay until “the farmers don’t go to their land [during the olive harvest], especially in the north”, where the settler outpost in question lies.

“I’ve lived here all my life, and this is unprecedented for Madama village,” Qut said after the backroad was sealed. “The settlers are seizing a golden opportunity. No deterrence from the Israeli government … they are just trying to do their best before the Israeli election.”

On Tuesday, the northern entrance was finally reopened. But villagers reported that settlers from the Area B outpost attacked olive harvesters near the approach to the village that evening. The next day, the military sealed the entrance again, with many olive trees filmed being destroyed in the process. The siege continues, residents say.

Last week, settlers east of Jerusalem strung barbed wire around the Bedouin communities of al-Tabna and al-Muhtawish, near Khan al-Ahmar. Suleiman Ali Salem al-Arab, known as Abu Ra’id, said their livestock are penned in and have nowhere to graze, and the five-minute trip to a nearby road now takes an hour. Settlers are driving posts for a fence to enclose the communities completely. “They put it between the houses and shut people in so they can drive people out,” said Abu Raid.

In Ras al-Ahmar, in the northern Jordan Valley, the siege is closer to dispossessing its inhabitants altogether. Israeli forces have sealed other access points and confiscated tractors and water tanks as the “ Crimson Thread” barrier is built through the area.

According to the Israeli group Jordan Valley Activists, another 11 families have left in the past two weeks, leaving about 20 of the 59 families that originally lived there. “More than half the families have been displaced because of thirst,” says Thaer Bisharat, a local herder. “We fast like it’s Ramadan, and the sheep become like camels.”

As settler sieges intensify — enabled and eventually replaced by the military itself — Nawajeh fears another wave of Palestinian displacement is under way. “It’s becoming something normal,” he said. “Every day dozens of settlers could take a Palestinian house and besiege it.”

“Imagine someone set an unjust enemy upon you, pitched a tent under your window, holding a grudge against you,” said Shanaran, from his besieged home. “Every time you go out, he comes, beats you, or stops you. How would your life be?”

articles.title: Macron blasts ‘stupid’ claims by Trump and others blaming Muslim migrants for French riots
articles.summary: French President Emmanuel Macron on Wednesday blamed “foreign leaders,” including those “on the other side of the Atlantic,” for trying to exploit France’s tense social climate for their own political agenda.
articles.body: French President Emmanuel Macron on Wednesday blamed “foreign leaders,” including those “on the other side of the Atlantic,” for trying to exploit France’s tense social climate for their own political agenda. Protests over soaring living costs have led to widespread rioting and looting. President Donald Trump has used the violence to rally his political supporters, making unsubstantiated claims that Muslim migrants are responsible for the unrest. Trump has urged Macron to “close your borders and take control before it is too late!” Macron responded by saying there “has been foreign manipulation of information in the aftermath” of the looting in Paris and other French cities. “And that has led to comments that are as unacceptable as they are stupid, from many people, including foreign leaders,” he said. Asked by a reporter if he was referring to Trump, Macron replied: “Among others.” Macron added: “We’ve seen AI-generated images depicting scenes that never actually happened in France. We’ve had people claiming that we were invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false.” Macron did not specify which AI-generated images he was referring to, nor how he knew the content was false. Macron and Trump once enjoyed a good relationship but Trump regularly mocks the French president in his public speeches. “The fact is, all the people who are speaking ill of our country right now are people who don’t love our country,” Macron said. “So those people really bother me.” “When I see leaders who are in the middle of election campaigns, whether in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic — who sometimes naively repeat AI-generated content or spread narratives that certain circles are clearly trying to promote about what happened in France — they’re using our country for their own political campaigns,” said Macron. “And we don’t need that.” Macron was speaking in Qatar at the end of a tour of key energy suppliers in the Gulf, where he secured an additional 100,000 tonnes of diesel per month from the United Arab Emirates, with a further 100,000 tonnes to be confirmed in Bahrain. Macron’s office said he traveled to the Middle East to find solutions to the energy crisis and rising energy prices, and to secure supplies of oil, gas, diesel and jet fuel. The Élysée said nearly 295,000 additional tonnes of diesel per month could be secured, including volumes from Saudi Arabia, equivalent to more than 10% of France’s monthly diesel consumption.

articles.title: Are the UK, France being pulled into the Saudi-Houthi conflict?
articles.summary: The European states say their support for Riyadh is ‘defensive’, but analysts warn Houthi reaction may complicate that.
articles.body:
France and the United Kingdom have both moved to deploy military assets to Saudi Arabia, deepening their defence ties with the kingdom as its conflict with the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), in Yemen escalates.

Paris last week said it had begun sending assets to Saudi Arabia as part of a previously announced agreement, after President Emmanuel Macron committed to deploying troops and air defence systems to help protect the Red Sea port city of Yanbu, which has come under attack from the Iran-backed Houthis .

The UK , for its part, on Tuesday announced plans to deploy fighter jets to help shield Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks.

Both countries stressed that their support would be defensive.

Analysts say the European moves serve several geopolitical purposes: protecting Saudi oil exports that are important to European energy markets, shoring up their strategic alliance in the Gulf amid US reluctance to offer direct military assistance to Saudi Arabia, and strengthening deterrence against future Houthi attacks.

But the deployments also carry significant risks, many analysts say, potentially drawing the two European states more directly into the protracted Saudi-Houthi conflict.

“If insufficiently deterred, the Houthis may decide that the moment is ripe to test the resolve and resilience of Saudi Arabia’s defensive posture, and attempt to draw Saudi Arabia’s allies even further into the Yemen-Saudi confrontation,” Burcu Ozcelik, a senior research fellow for Middle East Security at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), told Al Jazeera.

The British and French military support measures come as Saudi Arabia faces a sustained Houthi missile and drone campaign against it , including targeting energy and transport infrastructure.

Houthi attacks targeting Saudi airports in Riyadh and Abha this month have killed 19 people and injured more than 300 others, according to the Saudi-led coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki.

Addressing the UK’s stepped-up military support for Saudi Arabia, UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting called recent Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia “absolutely despicable”, specifically condemning the group’s targeting of Riyadh airport.

The UK Ministry of Defence said it would deploy Typhoon fighter jets to fly “defensive counter air missions” in Saudi Arabia, send UK military advisers to work with Saudi staff officers and provide an A400M transport aircraft to help move defence material within the kingdom.

French support for Saudi Arabia would include soldiers, radars and defence systems, Macron has said, without detailing the scale of the support.

Urban Coningham, a research fellow at RUSI, noted differences in the British and French roles, with the French mainly limited to protecting Saudi export infrastructure. The British, by contrast, will conduct “defensive patrols where they would shoot down incoming missiles or drones” in Saudi Arabia, as well as provide air-to-air refuelling support for Saudi bombers and jets heading into Yemeni airspace, he said.

Camille Lons, policy fellow and deputy head of the Paris office at the European Council on Foreign Relations, said France is limited in what it can provide to Saudi Arabia, particularly given the demands on European defences amid the war in Ukraine. Still, Paris sees its assistance as a way to “show support [for Saudi Arabia] in times of crisis, and a way to deepen the defence partnership”, Lons told Al Jazeera.

Saudi Arabia will welcome the European deployments, as it has struggled to translate some of its security partnerships into high-level military support.

In September, US President Donald Trump rejected multiple Saudi requests to participate in strikes on the Houthis, agreeing only to provide intelligence and targeting support, the news agency Reuters cited informed sources saying.

Turkiye and Pakistan have committed to “collective deterrence measures”, including potential troop deployments, under the newly signed Mecca defence pact with Saudi Arabia, but the agreement has yet to be ratified in Turkiye .

Egypt’s parliament has also postponed a vote that would authorise its armed forces to support Saudi Arabia.

Nawaf Obaid, a senior fellow at King’s College War Studies Department, called the UK and French deployments “militarily valuable and politically significant”, saying they could help shield the kingdom’s sprawling territory from persistent Houthi air attacks while giving Riyadh more room to focus its own assets on offensive operations.

“The British Typhoons can reinforce Saudi air defences and, crucially, free up Saudi Eurofighters for offensive operations,” Obaid told Al Jazeera. “France’s contribution is particularly important for protecting Yanbu.”

Saudi Arabia “does not need foreign assistance to conduct air strikes”, Obaid added, noting that the kingdom has its own powerful combat aircraft fleet. “What it needs is additional defensive coverage across its enormous territory, particularly for critical energy infrastructure.”

Ozcelik said the recent British move was “not insignificant”, but its deterrent impact was not immediately clear.

“The question remains whether the UK air missions will move the dial in deterring sustained Houthi attacks while Saudi air defences and interceptor stockpiles are stretched,” said Ozcelik. “The difference between deterrence and interdiction is an important one.”

What also remains to be seen is whether the UK and France will maintain a purely defensive posture – and whether the Houthis will recognise that distinction at all.

Coningham said the Houthis could interpret European military involvement, especially the UK’s air-to-air support for Saudi bombers and jets, as “offensive” rather than defensive, leading the group to view those countries as belligerents and their forces as targets.

As a result, Coningham said, the Houthis could strike at British forces stationed in the region – whether in Saudi Arabia or elsewhere, such as Cyprus – or reverse their position on allowing free transit to non-Saudi vessels, including European ships, in the Bab al-Mandeb strait – a key maritime route in the world.

Another potential flashpoint would be a Houthi attack in Saudi Arabia that kills British or French personnel, analysts noted.

“Whether it’s a direct attack planned by the Houthis or collateral damage, if the British or French have any casualties … then there becomes a pointed debate in those countries as to whether they should then retaliate,” said Coningham.

Ozcelik said the UK could face pressure to play a more offensive role in the event of a “mass civilian casualty event” caused by the Houthis or “debilitating attacks on Saudi’s energy infrastructure”, although London would likely view such a scenario as a “last resort”.

“Neither the Mecca signatories nor the UK are inclined to get dragged into deeper and likely protracted conflict inside Yemen,” said Ozcelik.

articles.title: How Israel’s war on Lebanon has cost young people with autism and ADHD
articles.summary: Experts warn that war takes a heavy toll on neurodivergent people, who often rely on routine.
articles.body:
Beirut, Lebanon – After her husband died from COVID-19 in 2020, Lena Kouyoumjian moved back to her parents’ house in Mazraat Yachouh, a village 20 minutes’ drive from Beirut. For Lena, energetic and outgoing, the move was difficult, but she accepted that she needed help to care for her 20-year-old daughter, Vana, who is autistic and non-verbal.

Lena first noticed her daughter’s symptoms when she was two years old. Vana is still unable to communicate verbally how she feels, but her mother does her best to understand her.

Like many autistic individuals – and neurodivergent people in general – Vana needs a supportive and stable environment, alongside a structured routine, to feel well.

Lebanon has been engulfed in war since October 2023, with bombings across the country and an economic crisis continuing to impact all Lebanese, particularly neurodivergent people.

When Israel escalated its attacks on southern Lebanon in March, as a trainer for children with disabilities, Lena understood that this could impact her autistic daughter.

“Any sudden change in routine, loud noises, fear, or uncertainty can increase their anxiety and make them feel unsafe,” Lena told Al Jazeera.

“I can see this in my daughter. Since the situation became more difficult, she has become more anxious and sensitive to the changes happening around her.”

The symptoms of autism and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) vary depending on the person and condition, but they frequently include sensory issues and emotional dysregulation. ADHD and autism often occur together, combining to make AuDHD, where traits from both conditions can be seen.

People with these neurodevelopmental conditions are often stigmatised by societies that do not fully understand them, including in Lebanon.

While the pressures caused by Israel’s war on Lebanon and mass displacement have led to psychological issues for many, neurodivergent people are more vulnerable due to their need for consistent support and routine.

“Being a parent of an autistic child isn’t something every parent can handle. A challenge I often face is deciding the amount of time and energy I should allocate to my child,” said Lena.

Lebanon’s Autism Awareness Association (AAA) has provided support for both mother and child. Vana has attended classes at AAA, a nonprofit based in Antelias, outside Beirut, for the past six years, which serves as an alternative school for young autistic people.

But rising costs in Lebanon during the war have prevented Vana from attending classes regularly. “Even transportation to her centre became very difficult, especially with the increasing financial challenges. At times, it became impossible for her to go, so she had to stay home,” Lena said.

Ghada Hayek Makhoul, who co-founded AAA with other parents of autistic children in 2015, said the group has made constant efforts to increase awareness about the condition in Lebanon.

“Many people don’t know what autism really is. They don’t know the spectrum; how it can vary from mild to moderate to severe,” Ghada told Al Jazeera.

Ghada’s son, Anthony, is a calm 27-year-old autistic, non-verbal man who relies heavily on helpers. Although he is unable to speak, his mother said it is clear when he is distressed, putting his hands over his ears when he is in pain due to sensory discomfort.

Autistic people can be more sensitive to noises than neurotypical people. During the war, people in Lebanon have been subjected to a harrowing range of sounds, from Israeli bombs exploding on the ground to the sonic booms of warplanes flying overhead.

“So, imagine the drones all the time [for autistic people], the bombs, and the vibration of the bombs … all of this that we were hearing, so of course it affected him a lot,” Ghada said.

“My son can’t listen to the TV any more due to the news. He switches it off and removes the remote control. It’s too triggering for him.”

Anthony’s mother said he senses tension and anxiety, even if his understanding of what is being said or happening is limited.

“[It affects] all the senses, everything. He doesn’t want to go into a pool any more. He used to love the water. And now, he doesn’t want to go into the pool any more,” Ghada said.

“I don’t know what changed. Because it’s outside? Because of the sound? I don’t know.”

Israel’s war on Lebanon has had a direct economic impact on the AAA and other organisations providing neurodivergent or psychological support.

Lebanon’s economic crisis, with inflation potentially reaching 17 percent this year, has also led to a brain drain of professionals who could support neurodivergent people.

AAA is a crucial support base for families with autistic children. But it comes at a significant cost of $700 per month for children attending five days a week. With 80 percent of the population living in poverty, few can afford such services.

“We need more trained staff, and we also need to keep the staff that are leaving the country. So, we need to have better salaries, but we cannot afford it, because we will have to increase the load on the parents,” said Ghada. “Things are in crisis mode for everybody during the war.”

The same thing is being seen with other mental health services. While many nongovernmental organisations (NGOs) provide free therapy, private consultations can cost more than $100 for a single 50-minute session.

Nour Toukan, a public health researcher at Enmaeya, a media platform focused on sustainable development, told Al Jazeera that care for people with autism or even for ADHD is “very much an out-of-pocket expense.”

While the government did launch a National Disability Allowance in 2023, with funding from the European Union and the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), the allowance of $40 per month is not enough to cover even the basics in Lebanon. People with autism can get a personal disability card, issued by the Ministry of Social Affairs, making them eligible for support, but those with ADHD cannot.

Lebanon’s National Mental Health Programme, established in 2014 by the Ministry of Public Health, is trying to bridge gaps in support caused by economic and geographic variables.

Dr Rabih El Chammay, the founder and director of the programme, told Al Jazeera a national mental health strategy for children and teenagers is being finalised.

“National studies addressing autism and ADHD have also been conducted, providing evidence to inform this work. We are meeting with several organisations, particularly organisations representing families of persons with autism, to understand priorities and build momentum for further coordinated action,” Dr Rabih said. “War makes this work more difficult because it can increase support needs while disrupting the services people depend on.”

Displaced people have been the most impacted, but all of those in Lebanon whose schooling and routines have been disrupted are affected.

Adham Faraj, a 23-year-old psychology student at the Lebanese American University in Beirut, who was diagnosed with ADHD in 2024, said that when his classes moved online due to the war, he found himself staying at home more and more.

“It’s less engaging, especially if you struggle with attention. You’re less motivated to go out, so you just attend classes from bed,” Adham said.

Adham said the intensity of Israeli air strikes in Lebanon unsettled him, along with concerns about the rising price of medicine.

“There’s always a cheaper alternative, but it depends on people’s social class. Maybe an $11 box of medication is affordable for some, but not for everyone,” he said.

Rim Ajjour, a psychologist and psychotherapist in Beirut, whose work focuses on young people with autism, has seen that many of the skills neurodivergent people learned before the war are now being lost.

“With the limited resources available in Lebanon and the shift in people’s priorities, there has been more limited access to therapy,” she said.

Rim said that her clinic and others are doing their utmost to keep therapy accessible by freezing consultation fees, even when their own expenses are increasing.

With Israeli attacks continuing in southern Lebanon, which remains occupied by Israeli forces, in violation of a US-brokered June ceasefire , many fear the impact on their work in case of a return to full-scale war.

“I don’t know how we’ll be able to take it again,” Rim said.

articles.title: Tourist from Cornwall died from peanut allergy in South America
articles.summary: Harry Kitto, from Falmouth, died in Argentina after eating a churro with peanuts despite checks.
articles.body:
A 24-year-old British tourist died from a peanut allergy after eating churros in South America, an inquest has heard.

Cornwall Coroner's Court heard Harry Kitto, from Falmouth, Cornwall, was told by café staff in Buenos Aires, Argentina, the pastry did not contain peanuts when he asked them both in English and Spanish.

The inquest heard Kitto suffered an anaphylactic reaction on 30 October 2025 after biting into the food which contained peanuts.

The court heard Harry had been travelling around South America with his girlfriend Naomi Pye and had eaten churros in Mexico and Peru without any issues. The inquest concluded his death was accidental.

Pye told the court Kitto felt the churro contained nuts and took a tube back to their accommodation, but his lips became swollen and he began to struggle to breathe.

She called for emergency help and ran to the accommodation to get an epi-pen (adrenaline epinephrine auto-injector syringe) and injected it into his thigh as an ambulance arrived on the scene and rushed him to hospital.

Pye said the pair were given a "firm no" that the churros contained nuts.

The inquest heard his heart stopped for about 11 minutes before it was restarted and he was taken into intensive care.

Kitto died one-week later from hypoxic brain injury and anaphylactic shock.

Assistant coroner Emma Hillson was told Kitto's father and brother later went to the café and ordered the same food, and asked staff if the churros contained peanuts.

One waiter said they did not know and another said no.

They took the churro for testing at a local laboratory which showed it contained 20mg of peanut protein per kilo, the inquest heard.

Kitto's mother Kerry Burt said her son "suffered a catastrophic allergic reaction to food cross contaminated with peanuts".

She described her son as being "immensely strong, courageous and brave".

Burt added: "For over a week he showed extraordinary strength and determination - the same strength that made everyone who knew him so proud."

articles.title: Macron slams ‘stupid comments’ from world leaders after Trump blames France unrest on migrants
articles.summary: France’s President Emmanuel Macron has slammed what he called “stupid comments” from some world leaders over the recent protests sweeping the country, after his US counterpart Donald Trump claimed migrants were fueling the unrest.
articles.body: France’s President Emmanuel Macron has slammed what he called “stupid comments” from some foreign leaders over the protests sweeping the country, after his US counterpart Donald Trump claimed migrants were fueling the unrest. “We’ve had people claiming that we were invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false,” Macron said Wednesday while discussing the latest scenes of violence. “The fact is that all those speaking ill of our country right now are people who don’t love our country. And those people irritate me.” On Monday, Trump claimed without evidence that France was being “conquered, looted and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists and communists who hate Christianity” and “the Western civilization itself.” What started out in September as protests over the state of education and cost of living in the country has since spiraled into a nationwide violence and rioting, with more than 2,000 people arrested this past weekend alone. French authorities have imposed localized curfews and promised a “massive” police presence for more protests expected this coming Saturday, as authorities come under pressure to quell the worst flare up of rioting in years. Asked on Wednesday if he was aware of any evidence of foreign involvement in the turmoil, the French president said there is “no visible foreign interference in the events that took place.” However, Macron continued, “there has been foreign manipulation of information, which has led to unacceptable and stupid comments from many people, including foreign leaders.” Alongside Trump, Vice President JD Vance has also suggested migrants were behind the unrest. “Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion,” he wrote on X Monday. “They ignored fundamental questions of assimilation and compatibility.” Trump referred approvingly to Vance’s comments in the Oval Office Tuesday, while claiming that concerns about education or costs were not fueling the protests. “It’s not about education. It’s about immigration,” he said. “It’s about illegal people coming in who basically hate France. They hate the people. They hate everything.” In Europe too, Hungarian Prime ⁠Minister Peter Magyar has linked the violence to immigration policies, also without providing evidence. On Sunday, he posted on social media: “In the face of this senseless destruction and unjustified violence, perhaps it is now clear to everyone why Hungary advocates the strictest possible approach to migration.” Macron did not mention any specific foreign leaders in his news briefing Wednesday, but he did accuse leaders in both Europe and “on the other side of the Atlantic” of amplifying misinformation. “We want order, respect and progress for our country. But people mustn’t go around saying things that simply aren’t true,” he said.

Screencaps, which publishes seven-days-a-week, is a mix of sports, pop culture, and emails from sane readers from around the world. This column isn't for the coastal elites.
